Together with the commentary.
In the first chapter, the first quarter.
Now, therefore, begins the inquiry into Dharma. || 1 ||

Those words which are well-known in common usage for certain meanings should be understood in the Sūtras as having those very same meanings, provided that this is possible; their meaning should not be imagined through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and the like, nor should they be assigned a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*). In this way, the Vedic sentences themselves—[are to be interpreted].

[Otherwise,] they would have to be explained; otherwise, the Vedic sentences would have to be explained, and their own constituent words would also have to be explained, which would result in an excessive burden (*prabalagaurava*). In that regard, this word "loka" is seen in the world to serve as a means for the derivation of what is not directly perceived, but nothing of the sort is observed here.

However, that [cause] must exist, in whose presence the desire to know Dharma (dharmajijñāsā) is conceived as occurring immediately thereafter; for in this way, its meaning becomes well-established, and that cause is the study of the Veda, since it is only when that exists that the former is conceived. [Objection: This is not so, for [the desire to know Dharma] might also arise from another action...
"Then it follows that the inquiry into Dharma is appropriate even before the study of the Veda. It is replied:

The Teacher employed the word *atha* with reference to an inquiry into Dharma such as I have in mind, which is not possible without the study of the Veda. How so? Because of the [reliance on] Vedic sentences—

A manifold investigation will be conducted here. Furthermore, the reading "atra" (here) is not appropriate; rather, the reading should be "iti" (thus). Regarding the term "prayajña," the Kāṇva Saṃhitā reads "sayajña."
--- Page 54 --- Mīmāṃsā-darśana 2.2.169–170: On the Non-Modification of Mantras in the Context of Animal Sacrifices.

The question is whether mantras used in animal sacrifices (paśu-yajña) are subject to modification (ūha) when the gender or number of the victim differs from the original form, or whether they remain unmodified. The opponent argues that since the animal sacrifice is a subsidiary (aṅga) of the Soma sacrifice, and since the Soma sacrifice involves the slaughter of many animals, the mantras should be modified according to the specific requirements of each individual animal. The Siddhāntin (concluding view) maintains that the mantras are not to be modified. The reason is that the animal sacrifice is a distinct ritual act (karma) performed for its own sake, and the mantras are prescribed specifically for that act. Since the animal sacrifice is a single unitary rite, even if multiple animals are sacrificed, the mantra remains fixed as it was originally enjoined for that specific ritual context. Therefore, no modification is required. Thus, the mantras are to be used exactly as they are recited in the archetype (prakṛti).

We learn from the text that there is a prohibition of the inquiry into Dharma prior to the study of the Veda, but not an injunction of immediate succession following it; nor can this single sentence both prohibit the inquiry into Dharma before the study of the Veda and enjoin its immediate succession after it, for in that case, the sentence would be split.
The statement is indeed twofold: for one part, occurring before the mention of Vedic study, prohibits the inquiry into Dharma; while another part, occurring after it, teaches immediate succession.
In the phrase "having studied the Vedas," in one instance the immediate succession is enjoined by way of restatement.

In the other case, it is the opposite; moreover, because they refer to the same subject matter, he will later explain their syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*). Furthermore, once the Veda has been studied, two things follow: one must return from the teacher’s house (*gurukula*) and one must investigate the sentences of the Veda. In that regard, [if it were said] "he returned from the teacher’s house," how then...

The purpose of this instruction is that one should investigate the sentences of the Veda. If this is so, then the prior study of the Veda would no longer be understood; for they prescribe thus: "Having studied the Veda, one should perform the ceremonial bath (snāna). And here [it is said]: "Having studied the Veda, being about to bathe and desiring to know Dharma..."

One should not transgress this traditional authority (āmnāya)! Nor is that which is called traditional authority something to be transgressed. To this it is replied: we shall indeed transgress this traditional authority, for by not transgressing it, we would conceive of the Veda as having a purpose—that is, as being meaningful—whereas its purpose is seen to consist in ritual action.
This is called "awakening. And that [awakening] does not arise from mere recitation; therefore, the ritualists do not declare a fruit for it.

Even regarding those cases where they seem to declare one, there the meaning is: "In the case of substances, purificatory acts, and rituals, because they are subservient to another purpose, the mention of a fruit must be an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda). Thus it is said.

He will state [this] when discussing the arguments. Nor is it the case that "this immediate succession to knowledge is enjoined for one who has studied the Veda. For there is no word whatsoever that expresses immediate succession to non-knowledge; rather, the suffix *ktvā* denotes anteriority in time, not immediate succession. Furthermore, the study [of the Veda] has a visible purpose.
[If it were taken literally,] it would contradict the immediate sequence [of study]; however, this meaning must be understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

For this knowledge is not enjoined for the sake of some unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*); rather, by secondary indication, the completion of the rule regarding ignorance and so forth is made simultaneous with the study of the Veda, as in: "Having studied the Veda, one should bathe."
‘Let him not return from the teacher’s house’—this is solely for the purpose of avoiding the unintended consequence (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
[The Kāṇva recension reads: “He will prohibit [it]”].
--- Page 55 --- Chapter 1,
Section 1 | Commentary (Bhāṣya): Therefore, having first completed the study of the Veda, one should thereafter desire to know Dharma.

—Thus is the force of the word *atha*. We do not say that the inquiry into dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) should not be undertaken immediately after some other action; rather, the meaning of the word *atha* is that having studied the Veda, one should not proceed in haste, but rather dharma should be inquired into immediately thereafter.
Therefore, [the statement] "I dwell in this place" is like [inferring] the heat of a water-pot from its steam;

because a reason for inquiry is observed, it follows that "thereafter, dharma is to be inquired into"—this is the power of the word. For one who has not studied the Vedic sentences in order to investigate dharma—
Since one would not be able to know the Veda [without it], for this reason, immediately thereafter, one should desire to investigate Dharma; such is the meaning of the word "therefore" (ataḥ).

The desire to know Dharma is *dharmajijñāsā*; for that is the wish to know it. How is it to be desired to be known? What is Dharma? What is its definition? What are its means of accomplishment? What are the fallacious means? And what is its ultimate purpose? Among these, first: what is Dharma? How...

The definition [of Dharma] has been explained by a single sūtra: "Dharma is a beneficial matter characterized by Vedic injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ*). What are its means of proof (*sādhana*), what are the fallacious means of proof (*sādhanābhāsa*), and what is its ultimate goal? These have been explained by the *Śeṣalakṣaṇa* (the section on subsidiary elements). Furthermore, where does the subservience to the human purpose lie, and who is that person (*puruṣa*)? [These questions are addressed in the subsequent sections.]

Is it a subordinate factor?—this is the summary aphorism for these propositions: "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*). [Objection: "Is Dharma well-known or not well-known?
If it is well-known, it need not be inquired into; if it is not well-known, it certainly cannot be inquired into. Thus, this [inquiry] is purposeless."

Is this section on the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) purposeful, or not? For many who are ignorant hold conflicting views regarding Dharma—some declare one thing to be Dharma, others another. One who acts while fallen into such doubt might fail to obtain what is beneficial and instead incur harm.
Therefore, Dharma is to be investigated; for we maintain that it indeed unites a person with the supreme good (niḥśreyasa). This is stated:
"Dharma is a purposeful object characterized by Vedic injunction (codanā). (1.1.2)
The Bhāṣya states: "The teachers say that 'codanā' is a statement that impels one toward action. (Mīmāṃsā-darśana, p. 56).

For it is observed that one who is impelled thinks, "I shall do it. That by which something is characterized is its defining purpose (tattvārtha); for they say that smoke is the mark (lakṣaṇa) of fire. Likewise, we maintain that whatever is thus characterized is the purpose that unites a person with the supreme good (niḥśreyasa). For an injunction (codanā) indeed pertains to what is existent (bhūta),...

It is capable of making known such objects as those that are past, future, subtle, concealed, or remote; nor is its expression excessively disordered; nor does the injunction (codanā) speak of a relationship in the manner of some common worldly statement, such as "on the bank of the river... [and so forth].

"Fruits exist"—this [statement] occurs even in that case, yet it may also be false. It is said in reply: this which is stated—"he speaks falsely"—is contradictory. "He speaks" means he causes understanding (it is the cause for one who is understanding).
[It is said: "it comes to be. That which, being present as a cause, brings about awakening, is what causes one to understand.

And if it is understood from the injunction that heaven results from the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, how can it be said that "it does not happen thus"? Or, if it is the case that "it does not happen thus," [then the injunction is false].

How is it that one does not understand? To say that one understands an object that is non-existent is a contradiction. Furthermore, from the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," nothing uncertain is understood, such as whether heaven exists or does not exist; nor is anything [uncertain] understood even when [the matter] is already certain.

This notion would be false if, having arisen, it were to perish—[thinking] "this is not so"—for that is a false cognition; yet this [notion of the Self] does not undergo subversion at another time, in another person, in another state, or in another place. Therefore, it is non-false. As for that which...

Worldly speech that comes from a trustworthy person, or that concerns an object of the senses, is indeed non-false; however, that which comes from an untrustworthy person, or that which concerns an object beyond the senses, is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) as it originates from human intellect. For that [Vedic word] is non-human (*apauruṣeya*), and it is appropriate for humans to know it.

[The opponent says: "Because of the statement: 'That object is understood from the non-human [Veda] because there is no human statement [to the contrary]'. If this is argued, that too is equal to the previous point; for in matters of this kind, the word of a person does not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*), just as the speech of those born blind has no authority regarding specific colors. Furthermore, even a learned man cannot deny [this].

One does not conceive [of it as such], even though it is being taught; and since Manu and others have understood it from that person, it is known through perception alone, just as form is perceived by the eye. It is said in reply: for teachings may arise even from delusion, and they fall away...
--- Page 57 --- Chapter 1, Section 1 || 5 Bhāṣya: Even from the Veda, there may be delusion.
"A person knows the three"— this is a cognition based on common experience, not a Vedic statement.

The inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is as follows: when a human statement is understood to be false, this [Vedic statement] is also understood to be false, because it is not something else;
for the falsity of one thing cannot entail the falsity of another, precisely because it is different—just as [the falsity of Devadatta’s speech does not imply the falsity of Yajñadatta’s].
Just as Yajñadatta’s being dark implies that his son must also be dark; furthermore,

the inference that "the Vedic word is false because it shares the same nature as human speech" is understood through the observation of others, whereas the conviction regarding the Vedic word arises from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and inference is not [equivalent to] direct perception.

[The opponent's view is that] there is a contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, [the question arises: "Is it not rather the object characterized by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) that should be investigated? What is the use of investigating *dharma*? It is replied: That very thing which brings about the highest good (*śreyaskara*) is what is denoted by the word *dharma*. How is this to be understood?
For indeed, one who performs a sacrifice is designated as "righteous" (*dhārmika*);
whatever a person is the agent of, he is designated by that term, just as one who cooks is called a "cook" (*pāvaka*) and one who reaps is called a "reaper" (*lāvaka*).
Therefore, that which unites a person with the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is denoted by the word *dharma*. Not [otherwise].

In the world alone, but even in the Veda—as in "By means of sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the Sacrifice; those were the first dharmas"—they teach that dharma is precisely what is denoted by the word *yajati* (he sacrifices).
Here, both are indicated by the injunction (*codanā*): the beneficial and the harmful. What is the beneficial?

That which leads to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and so forth. What is "non-benefit" (*anartha*)? That which leads to transgression (*pratyavāya*), such as the *Śyena*, *Vajra*, *Iṣu*, *Bhr̥t*, *Aivāma*, and others. In that context, the term "benefit" (*artha*) is included so that it may not be said that non-benefit is also Dharma. But how is this [the Śyena, etc. a non-benefit? Because it is indeed violence (*hiṃsā*).

"And violence is prohibited. But how, then, can that which is harmful be taught as something to be performed? It is said: the *śyena* and other such rites are not understood as being themselves to be performed; rather, their instruction is to the effect that "for one who wishes to cause harm, this is the means"—thus it is with the *śyena*.
For they recite: "One should not sacrifice while practicing sorcery," but not: "Sorcery should be practiced.
Now, it might be argued: "This aphorism is not explicitly heard [in the scripture] to express these two meanings—the injunction...
[Page 58]
In the Mīmāṃsā system (Bhāṣya):
Dharma is characterized by [the Veda], not by the senses and so forth; it is the purposeful, not the purposeless;
for this is a single sentence, and it would be split if it were otherwise. It is said: "And that which..."

The meaning is understood from a sentence; and if that were the case, it would apply to Vedic texts, but not to the Sūtras. For when the meaning is already understood from another source, one understands the Sūtra as being "for this purpose. And because they are "strung together" (sūtryante) as parts [of a larger whole], they are called Sūtras. In that regard, there is no difference between two distinct sentences.

It should be understood that [the word] "deśa" (place) is used here. Alternatively, since it is stated that dharma is that which exists and is characterized by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*), the meaning is indeed the same. Sūtra: 3. *Tatsya nimittaparīṣṭiḥ* (The investigation of its cause).
Bhāṣya: We have stated that "the knowledge of dharma has its source in injunction" (*codanā*).

That was stated as a mere proposition; now we shall examine its source—whether it is injunction alone, or something else as well. Therefore, he considers that [the matter] is not yet determined by this much alone: "Injunction..."

"Dharma is an object characterized by its marks"—thus it has been said. To this, the Sūtra replies: "The arising of cognition when a person's sense organs are in contact with their objects is perception; it is not the means [for knowing Dharma], because it is the apprehension of what is presently existing. (NS 1.1.4)

Bhāṣya: This is now examined—first of all, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not the means [of knowing Dharma]. What is the reason? For it is defined as such: "Perception is the arising of cognition in a person when there is contact of the sense organs with an existing object" (*sati indriyārthasambandhe yā puruṣasya buddhirjāyate, tat pratyakṣam*). [That is to say, it is the cognition that arises in a person when there is a connection between the sense organ and its object.]

Furthermore, this object will exist [in the future], yet it does not exist at the time of cognition; moreover, this apprehension pertains to what exists, not to what does not exist. Therefore, perception is not the sole means [of valid knowledge]. This sūtra is not intended to determine that any one of these—whether cognition, its arising, or sensory contact—is the defining factor; for [perception] exists...

It is determined that [perception occurs] only when there is contact between the sense-faculties and their objects; otherwise, if many [factors] were being enjoined here, the sentence would be split. Furthermore, because inference, comparison, and presumptive testimony are preceded by perception, they too lack the status of being independent causes [of knowledge].
Since even non-existence does not exist: --- Page 59 --- Chapter 1, Section 1.

But the relationship between a word and its meaning is innate; the knowledge thereof arises from instruction, which is non-deviant regarding an object not perceived [by other means]. That is authoritative for Bādarāyaṇa because of its independence. || 5 ||

Bhāṣya: We say that it is "eternal" (*autpattika*). For "origination" (*utpatti*) is used figuratively to denote "existence" (*bhāva*). The relationship between word and meaning is an inseparable existence; it is not a relationship that occurs subsequently after both have been produced. And this relationship of the word with its meaning is eternal; of that [the fire... *Note: The text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the example of the word "fire."*
[It is] the cause of dharma characterized by the *hotṛ* and other [priestly functions], which is not apprehended through perception and the other [means of knowledge].
How so? Because there is "instruction" (*upadeśa*); for "instruction" is the utterance of a specific word.
It is not [the cause] of non-differentiated knowledge, for the knowledge produced from that [word]— (No English translation provided for the fragmentary Sanskrit text following.)
Regarding the term "non-erroneous" (*aviparyaya*): that which is indeed non-erroneous knowledge cannot be said to be "this is not so";
for it does not happen otherwise than as it is cognized, nor is it such that it is not cognized as it is. It would be a case where one thing is in his heart and another is on his lips.
For one who speaks thus, this contradiction is perceived—namely, that it both exists and does not exist.

Therefore, that [scriptural] authority need not be further scrutinized; for when this is the case, no other cognition or even another person need be relied upon, since this very cognition is supreme. The mention of Bādarāyaṇa is for the sake of [showing] respect...
This is stated as the opinion of Bādarāyaṇa in order to honor him, not to set forth his own personal view.
The author of the *Vṛtti*, however, explained this passage differently:

“Regarding [the sūtra] ‘the examination of its cause’ (*tasya nimitta-parīkṣā*), and so forth—it is not necessary to examine the cause, for perception and the other [means of knowledge] are well-established as the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and scripture (*śāstra*) is included within them; therefore, that too [need not be examined].”

It must be examined. To this it is said: one should examine it by means of its practical efficacy (*abhicāra*), because mother-of-pearl appears as if it were silver; therefore, perception is fallible, and since inference and the other means of knowledge are rooted in it, they too are fallible. Thus, one who proceeds toward an object based on such immediate apprehension...

It might be frustrated and might sometimes meet with misfortune; this is not so—since it is directly perceived, or rather, there is a reading: "not separated by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇayā*)."
In the Mīmāṃsā system (Bhāṣya):
That which does not deviate [from its object] is perception; that which deviates is not perception.
What, then, is perception? "When there is contact with that [object], the arising of cognition in a person through the sense organs is true perception.
That is to say, when there is contact of the sense organs with the very object whose cognition it is, the arising of cognition in a person is true perception;
whereas that cognition which arises from contact with one thing regarding another object is not [true perception].

[This is] perception. But how is this understood? That "this [cognition occurs] when there is contact with that," and "this [cognition occurs] when there is no contact with that"? Because that which does not occur when there is contact with something else occurs when there is contact with that very thing; the opposite of this is contact with something else. How is this to be known? [For example,] even in the case of mother-of-pearl, [there is the cognition] of silver.
"Thinking [it is silver], one considers, 'My eye is in contact with silver. For when a subverting cognition arises—'This is not so;

it is a false cognition'—that [occurs] when there is contact with something else, whereas the opposite occurs when there is contact with that [very thing]. How is this understood prior to the arising of the subverting cognition?"
When, at that time, there is no distinction whatsoever between right knowledge and false knowledge—

namely, when the mind is affected by the eyes and other [senses], or the sense organ is affected by cataracts and the like, or the object is affected by distance and so forth— then false knowledge arises. Subsequently...
For when [the causes] are impaired, there is false knowledge; indeed, the contact between the sense organs, the mind, and the object is the cause of right knowledge.
In its absence, there is false knowledge; the defect residing in either of those two is the cause of false knowledge.
For when they are defective, knowledge becomes false. How so?
Is it understood? Because we observe agreement once the defects have been removed. If it is asked, "How is the presence of defects understood?

[the answer is: If, despite searching with effort, we do not perceive a defect, we shall consider it to be non-defective due to the absence of any means of knowledge [to the contrary]. Therefore, for whomsoever the instrument is defective, and in whatever case...
The notion that "it is false" is itself an incorrect cognition, and no other.

Now, one might object: "Every cognition is indeed without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), for the nature of cognition as being without an objective basis is observed in dreams; it is the same for waking cognitions as well."
Whether it be the cognition "pillar" or "wall," it is indeed a cognition;

therefore, that too must be without an objective basis (nirālambana). It is replied: how can the well-ascertained cognition that arises as "pillar" be established as an error? [As for the case of] a dream—

"Even that [dream experience] was likewise perfectly determined, and there is no difference between it and the waking state prior to awakening. No, because in dreams one perceives errors; whereas in the waking state there is no error—page 61.
Chapter 1, Section 9.

[The opponent says: It must be requested in the other case as well. [The proponent replies: If it is argued that "because it is common to both, it will also occur in the other," then if the status of being a cognition (*pratyayatva*) is a false state for what is not a cognition, it ought to be likewise for a cognition that is currently arising. In this regard, "the appearance [of the cognition] is the cause for its being so."

It cannot be said that "this other [dream] is not a cognition" because it lacks causal conditions; for the falsity of one's own cognition in dreams and the like is observed even in the absence of external objects. If it is asked, "Why?"—it is because sleep is the cause of the falsity [of cognition] due to the weakness of the mind when it is accompanied by drowsiness.

And regarding one's own delusion: in deep sleep there is indeed an absence of dissolution, for it is precisely because of a lack of cognition that one is called "deeply asleep. Therefore, the cognition of one who is awake is not false. [Objection: But might there also be a defect of the instruments (the senses) even for one who is awake? [Reply: If there were such a defect, it would be perceived! [This is true] even at the time of seeing a dream.
If it is argued that [the self] is not understood as such, [we reply]: one who has awakened indeed understands, "My mind was overcome by sleep.
But [if you say the self is] void, how so? We do not perceive any difference in form between the object and the cognition thereof.

Furthermore, our intellect is a protector [of the object]; therefore, we see that there is no such thing as an "object-form" distinct from it. This might be so if the intellect possessed the form of the object; however, for us, the intellect is formless, whereas the object is external, for it is perceived as being connected with the outside.

It is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For perceptual cognition has an object as its domain, not another cognition; for it is momentary and does not persist until the time of another cognition.
"While it is itself arising, it is known and it makes another object known, like a lamp."
If this were said, [we reply]: in that case, no one perceives the object through cognition when it is unknown;

rather, once it is known, one understands it through inference. Therefore, simultaneity is untenable. [Objection: Is it not the case that "the object is known" is said precisely while the cognition is arising, and not when it has not yet arisen? Therefore...

"First the cognition arises, and afterwards the object is known. True; first the cognition arises, but here [the opponent objects that] there is no "apprehension" (pratyeti). (Note: The Kāśmīra recension adds the word "iti" here.)
† The reading in the Kāśmīra recension (Kā0 Śrī0) is "pratyayāt".
"Arrived by the power of the transformation of poison," as found in the Prācīna-puṣpikā.
"Because of the perception of error both at the beginning and at the end of a dream, there is indeed an absence of deep sleep," so says the *Kārikā-saṃgraha*.
--- Page 62 --- 10 Mīmāṃsā-darśana (The Mīmāṃsā System)
But [in the case of] mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), it is known beforehand. For this sometimes occurs:

that which is impossible to know is called "unknown. Moreover, there is no apprehension of the form of cognition without its being designated. Therefore, cognition is designatable; and what is undesignatable is not perception.

Therefore, cognition is not perceptible. Moreover, even if cognition were of a single form, it would simply mean the non-existence of cognition itself, not the non-existence of the object which is directly perceived.
Nor is there a single form; for we infer cognition precisely by means of its manifestation, and we understand the object as possessing a form through direct perception itself.
Therefore, cognition has an object as its support. Furthermore, the cognition of a cloth has a fixed cause when only threads are being employed;
otherwise, even when threads are being taken up, a person with impaired senses might occasionally have the notion of a jar. But this does not happen; therefore, [cognition] is not without an object.
The object is the condition; therefore, direct perception does not deviate from its object.

Inference (*anumāna*) is the cognition of an object not in contact with the senses, based on the perception of one part of a known relationship. It is of two kinds: that in which the relationship has been perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣatodṛṣṭasaṃbandha*), and that in which the relationship has been perceived through generalization (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭasaṃbandha*). An example of inference where the relationship has been perceived through direct observation is the cognition of fire from the sight of smoke.

Cognition (*vijñāna*) is [knowledge] whose relation is based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*). For example, having perceived Devadatta’s arrival at another location preceded by his movement, one recollects the movement of the sun. Scripture (*śāstra*) is the cognition of words.
It is the cognition of an object not present to the senses. Analogy (*upamāna*) is also [the cognition of similarity] regarding an object not present to the senses.

It produces cognition, just as the sight of a *gavaya* [produces] the recollection of a cow. Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is also the postulation of a fact on the grounds that "a seen or heard matter is otherwise inexplicable";
for example, when Devadatta is known to be alive, the observation of his absence from the house leads to the unseen knowledge of his being outside.

[This is] conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Furthermore, the absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) regarding the non-existence of something not in contact [with the senses], namely the meaning "it does not exist"—since this is well-known, it need not be examined.
Now, let it be granted that perception and the others are indeed other means of valid cognition; however...

But verbal testimony is not a means of valid cognition. Why? "Because it is not a cause [of knowledge], since it apprehends what is already existent" (Sūtra 1.1.4). Verbal testimony is not a cause [of valid knowledge] (i.e., it is not a means of valid cognition), because its object is that which is already apprehended.
In this context, it is appropriate that the reading should be "na pratyakṣam" (not by perception).
"Of the living Devadatta," according to the Kāśikā Saṃgraha.
But this [verse] concludes the preceding verse; it is in the 19th line, at the 9th [position].
--- Page 63 --- Chapter 1, Section 1 ||

That which is not perceived does not exist, just as the horn of a rabbit. Furthermore, the sense organs of cattle and other animals are indeed perceptive, yet after the sacrifice for cattle, the cattle do not [reappear].
[They] are obtained! Therefore, the sacrifice does not have cattle as its fruit. Furthermore, the fruit must exist at the time of the ritual action;

for that which is the crushing [of the grain] occurs at that time, the pleasure of the crushing occurs at that time. If it is argued, "The fruit may arise at another time," we say: no. We understand that "the fruit of the sacrifice does not occur at another time."
Why? Because when that [past action] existed, it did not give its fruit;
and when the fruit arises, that [action] no longer exists. How can that which is non-existent give [a fruit]?

"— it is understood that [the word] causes a *prasaṅga* (an unwanted consequence)— this is known from the capacity of the cognition of the meaning;

Thus the purpose is stated: as many words as [constitute] a single purpose— Page 216—
In the Mīmāṃsā system,
as many [words] as accomplish a single purpose constitute one sentence; and here there are not many purposes, for there is no single word that can enjoin multiple intended objects.

Regarding the phrase "in the *revatī* verses," this is not merely an injunction for the *revatī* verses themselves; rather, it is "the *vāravantīya* [sāman] in the *revatī* verses. Here too, in these two words, the two instances of the word *vāravantīya* ending in the accusative case do not terminate in a mere relationship, but [signify] something additional to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

Now, because it exceeds [the requirements], it concludes with a mere connection to the act of "doing" (*karoti*), and then states the connection to the ultimate purpose. Thus, the *yajati* (sacrifice) as thus qualified is not for the sake of another; rather, that alone is the purpose of these constituent elements (*padārtha*). Therefore, there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*). However, if a fruit were to be postulated for the accessory (*guṇa*)—such as *agni*—[it would follow otherwise].
If it were the case that "the Vāravantīya is to be performed as the Agniṣṭoma-sāman of this [sacrifice]," there would be a syntactical split (vākya-bheda).
Now, if it is argued that the sacrifice itself— as qualified by all the attributes beginning with "in the Revatī verses"— is what is connected to "this Agniṣṭoma-sāman" [of the sacrifice]...
Even so, because of the connection with the desire for cattle (*paśukāma*), the sentence would be split.

If it were argued, "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with this *vāravantīya* chant performed over the *revatī* verses," that cannot be; for due to the introduction of a different [melodic] interval (*cagaantara*) and the loss of the specific [quality], there would be a deficiency in the subordinate element (*guṇya*).

“But was it not just said: ‘Indeed, it is possible to perform the Vāravantīya on the Revatī verses’? [The reply is: It is possible when there is an explicit injunction; in the absence of an injunction, they are not included by the mention of the Vāravantīya. “In that case, there will be an injunction: ‘One desiring cattle [should perform it] on the Revatī verses with the Vāra-’”
"One should perform the Vāravantīya upon the Revatī verses, and then one should sacrifice"—here, the term "sacrifice" (*yajati*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
If there is a statement regarding the connection between the Revatī verses and the Vāravantīya, then a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*) is established;

it is not an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) for the already praised [sacrifice]. [Objection: But surely, in the phrase "then one should sacrifice," there is a restatement of the sacrifice...
"Through the sacrifice, there will be a connection for this [desire] with such a purpose. This cannot be so;

for if it were enjoined as a subordinate element (aṅga) in relation to the sacrifice, there would be no connection with one who desires cattle. Or, if there were a connection with both, the sentence would be split (vākyabheda). "Now, the connection with the sacrifice is a restatement (anuvāda), by virtue of the context (prakaraṇa)..."
This is not tenable; for a direct statement (*vākya*) is more authoritative than the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Therefore, this is a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*), or else it is the *vāravantīya* chant performed upon the *revatī* verses as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) of a sacrifice, or a sacrifice characterized by that [chant].

We perceive the gender as a case-ending, but not [the gender] of the connection between the Revatīs and the Vāravantīya.

Thus says Mādhava.
Distinction

[The opponent says: A connection is made [between the *hīṣ* and the result], namely: "One desiring cattle should perform [the rite] with 'hīṣ'";

The second desire is thus: "In this way, there will be an abundance of fruit; therefore, there is another desire at the conclusion."
[Sūtra 26: "Because it is desired for everything, there should be a scriptural mention of desire with respect to that; however, the repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of the *nidhana*.

In the Mīmāṃsā system, the Bhāṣya states: "The specific determination of the meanings of words is the meaning of the sentence. This has been expressed [in Sūtra 1.1.25]:
"The recitation of those [words] which have attained that state [of mutual expectancy] with a word denoting action is for the sake of the purpose, because that [purpose] is caused by them."
"In that case, the sentence-meaning is again inferential by means of the word-meanings such as the denotative [word] and so forth; this is understood as follows:
that which is heard in its own isolated meanings and lacks direct application enters into syntactic unity with another proximate word, and not otherwise."

— thus, in this case, if the word *ekāhāyanī* (one-year-old cow), being connected with the verb *krīṇāti* (buys), has its purpose fulfilled and does not require a connection with another word, while the word *aruṇa* (red), failing to obtain a connection with another word, would be meaningless— then [the conclusion is that] the one-year-old cow...

It attains syntactic unity with the word [‘purchase’]. Now, it was argued: “Its purpose is to connect with the action, not to connect with the redness. To this he replies: “In order to avoid the word ‘red’ being rendered meaningless, its purpose is to connect with both.”

—so we say; for even that which is performed for one purpose is capable of being used for another purpose, just as, for example, channels are constructed for a field, yet from them water is both drunk and used for ritual sipping (upaspṛśyate). In the same way here too, the word *ekāhayanī* [is used] for the sake of its connection with the purchase (*kraya*).
"Being uttered, it will be connected with the word *aruṇā*; nothing is faulty [in this].

Therefore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). This is not so; for even if the word *ekāhayanī* were not to become meaningless, and thus [the term *aruṇā*] were to be connected with the *ekāhayanī*, nevertheless, in every case...
It ought to be placed in the manner [of the rule], yet this word "he does not purchase this Soma" is unable to qualify it;
for it is not uttered as a qualifier,
but rather it is enjoined as a novel (apūrva) matter.

"But surely, even when enjoining a previously unknown matter, it will be connected with the other [term], just as in the case of the word *ekahāyanī*. How so? For a word being uttered for a specific purpose is understood to serve that very purpose; thus, it relates to what is proximate in the mind."
"Therefore, by that [word] which is present in the intellect, the expectant word can be connected"—this is not so.
For that which, when not being connected, would be meaningless, that is what is connected, and nothing else. Why is this? Because when it is being connected, the universal (sāmānya) [is understood].
If it were established as a specific [rule], then the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) would be contradicted by the syntactical connection (*vākya*). And this is not the case—
Chapter 3, Section 1, Part 3.
Being unconnected with the verb "to buy," it would be meaningless; therefore, it shall be connected with the one-year-old cows mentioned in the context.

"Now, has it not been stated that even in the context (*prakaraṇa*), its connection is untenable? It is not untenable; for when one meaning is being enjoined within a single sentence, it cannot be connected with another due to a failure in the expressive power of the words, since the expressive power of the word regarding that which is being enjoined is indeed different.

When something is connected with a quality, the object being enjoined is made known as if it were unknown, whereas it is restated (anūdya) as if already known for the purpose of connecting it with a quality. Furthermore, a single word— such as the word *ekahāyanī*— cannot simultaneously be both "as if known" and "as if unknown" when it is uttered together [with other words].

When enjoined in relation to the act of purchase, it would be as if unknown; when connected with the word *aruṇā* (red), it is as if known. Furthermore, there is no fault in a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), for while other actions and other substances have been enjoined and obtained through other sentences within the context (*prakaraṇa*), this [present] is enjoined by another sentence.

It is connected [to the sacrifice], and that [quality] is enjoined with respect to one thing while being restated (anūdyate) with respect to another in the sentence; thus it becomes logically consistent. Therefore, due to the distinction of connection and the lack of distinction in the context (prakaraṇa), there is an application [of the quality] to all substances within the entire context.

This being the case, we reply: "When there is unity of purpose, there should be a restriction because of the single function of the substance and the quality. "I shall eat what has been offered to him"—thus [it is said]. In this regard, there is a doubt: Is "May Bhadra and the others be satisfied" and so forth one mantra, and "The Vasus, Bhadra and the others" another? Or is "Bhadra and the others" up to "I shall eat" one single mantra? What, then, is the prima facie view? That there are two.

There are two mantras, for these are two distinct parts; satisfaction is one thing and eating is another, and therefore, due to this difference in purpose, there is a split in the sentence. As it has been said: "Because its form and description [indicate] that the meaning [of the word] is enjoined as something to be set aside."

This being the case, we reply: because of the mention of a quality, the mantra and so forth should pertain to a single consumption; for satisfaction is mentioned as a qualification of the act of consuming, as in the words, "I consume; may my speech be satisfied."
"Now, [one might object]: 'Is it not the case that "tṛpyatu" (let him satisfy) is one word and "tarṣet" (he may thirst) is another?
This [latter] occurs as a future action serving as a secondary word (upapada).
In that case, there is a connection between two actions, namely: "I shall eat" and "speech may thirst."'"
Furthermore, in this case, there is no connection [of the word] "may he be satisfied" with the act "I eat.
It is said in reply: This [word] "may he be satisfied" is not understood as an injunction (*vidhi*). Then what?
It is used either in the sense of a prayer (*prārthanā*) or at the time of eating (*prāsa*), as in: "If I eat, may my speech be satisfied."

Thus, the connection is made as follows: "If I eat, it is the time for the casting [of the die] at the thirst for speech. Because of this relationship of qualifier and qualified, when there is a single purpose and a single sentence, it is appropriately established by the auspicious [words]. [Objection: But these two sentences are already devoid of expectancy (nirākāṅkṣe).

"Having split the form, they are made to have expectancy. To this it is replied: even if these two sentences were to express two distinct meanings that are independent and lack mutual expectancy, nevertheless, since the visible purpose is the manifestation of the act of eating (*bhakṣaṇa*) and not that of satiation (*tarpaṇa*), there is indeed a single unified purpose.

How much more so, then, when its status as a subordinate element (*guṇa*) is being understood? Therefore, because it denotes a subordinate quality, the mantra and other elements should constitute a single consumption—thus [is the conclusion]. (3.2.10 a0)

Is there to be consumption with the *bhakṣaṇamantra* for those offerings not dedicated to Indra? What, then, is the prima facie position?

That there is consumption with the *bhakṣaṇamantra* for those not dedicated to Indra. Why? Because the offerings are governed by the same injunctions, and among them, the mantra "of that drunk by Indra" (*indrapītasya*) is incapable of applying to what has not been drunk by Indra.

It cannot be said that the word *jahā* is possible within the same context, because in the absence of an explicit statement, it would denote something else. Therefore, in such cases, there is only the eating of the *bhramannaka*. Thus [the conclusion].

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is prescribed: "One desiring cattle should fetch [the water] with a milking vessel (godohana)," and likewise: "Having poured the broth of the animal at the Upamīya sacrifice, a post made of Bilva wood should be used by one desiring spiritual luster. Regarding such cases, there is a doubt.

—Should it be applied in the archetype (prakṛti) or in the ectype (vikṛti)? What is the prima facie view? That it belongs to the ectype; for [the archetype] is already satisfied by means of the vessel and the broth associated with the archetype. This being the position, we reply: the occasional (naimittika) element is inserted in the archetype, because of its connection with a specific occasion (nimitta).

Because of the general injunction, the *khadira*, *pālāśa*, and *rohitaka* woods are mentioned without distinction in the rule for the *camasa* cups; however, the *godohana* and *vailva* vessels are specifically enjoined. And a specific injunction overrides a non-specific injunction. Context is the general, while connection with a specific occasion (*nimitta*) is the particular.

That which is obtained in a general sense is indirect (*parokṣa*) by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); however, that which is obtained in a specific sense is direct (*pratyakṣa*) by way of primary denotation (*śruti*). And primary denotation is stronger than secondary indication, and the direct is stronger than the indirect. Therefore, it should apply only to the archetype (*prakṛti*). (Sūtra 3.6.3)
The section concerning the procedure for the *pavamāna* [stotras] in the *ādhāna*.
Sūtra: The establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) is for the purpose of the sacrifice (iṣṭi), because of the context (prakaraṇa). (Pūrvapakṣa)

There are the Pavamāna-iṣṭis: "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pavamāna," "to Agni Pāvaka," and "to Agni Śuci. In the context (prakaraṇa) of these, it is recited: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in the spring. Regarding this, there is a doubt:
Is the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) for the purpose of the Pavamāna offerings, or not? What is the prima facie view?
— [Page 423] — Chapter 3, Section 6.
Bhāṣya: "For the sake of the sacrifice"—why? Because of the context; it is heard in the context of those [offerings], therefore it is for their sake.
Sūtra: Or rather, not so; because they have that as their purpose. (Siddhānta)

The Pavamāna-iṣṭis are indeed for the sake of the fire (Agni). If Agni were for the sake of the iṣṭis, then that which is for the sake of the fire would benefit the iṣṭis. However, let the iṣṭis be fruitless;
consequently, even that which is for the sake of the fire would be fruitless. But how, then, is it for the sake of the fire?

Regarding the Pavamāna sacrifices: because they would otherwise be purposeless, whereas the fires themselves possess a purpose, the Pavamāna sacrifices should be performed even after the fires have been produced. Therefore, the Pavamāna sacrifices are not for the sake of the fires.
Sūtra: And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (Pūrvapakṣa) 23.
The indicative mark (liṅga) is seen, namely: "The Pavamāna-iṣṭis are for the sake of the first offerings.

What is the indicative mark? "This animal, the fire that has been established, indeed decays; therefore, one should offer these very oblations of the first offering at the end of a year; by that, it does not decay."
"By that very [act], he makes it new again; therein it is offered"—thus [it is said]. (6.4.1)
The section concerning the universal purpose of the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires).
Sūtra: That [is] for the sake of refuting that, just as other discourses not commenced [in this context] [are]. [Pūrvapakṣa] 23.

Bhāṣya: Regarding this *ādhāna* (the laying of the sacred fires), there arises a doubt: is it for a specific purpose (*pratyartham*), or is it for the sake of all ritual acts (*sarvakarmārtham*)? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It is said: it is for a specific purpose. Why? Because, just as other *anārabhyavāda* (independent) injunctions are for specific purposes, it is for that very same reason.
Sūtra: Or rather, it is for all purposes, because the installation has its own specific time. (Siddhānta)

The Bhāṣya states: "Or rather, the establishment [of the fires] (ādhāna) is for the sake of all ritual acts. What is the meaning? The meaning is that the establishment is for the sake of the substance of the fire which serves the purpose of all ritual acts, and it is not to be performed separately for each individual purpose. No suffix denoting a specific purpose is heard in the original injunction;
nor—" Page 424 —.
In the Mīmāṃsā system (Bhāṣya),
this [is established] by means of direct statement and the other [criteria].
In discussions concerning those [rites] not specifically commenced [for a particular purpose], they establish their status as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) for the sake of completion.
[The question arises: "Are these [rites] subsidiaries of the primary action (*prakṛti*) or of knowledge (*vidyā*)? Therefore, in those cases, it is well [established].
However, this [fact] is not a reason for subsidiarity; therefore, the installation of the fires (*ādhāna*) is not [a subsidiary] in that sense.
It is employed for ritual action and has all ritual actions as its purpose; it is "foremost"—thus it is called "the purpose of all.
Moreover, its time is prescribed by itself; that [time] need not be separately enjoined:
when the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma occurs, then this must be performed; and at that time...
By means of the spring seasons. Thus, when the performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices takes place, then it should be performed;

that is, on either the full moon day or the new moon day. However, for the purpose of non-omission, it is not performed during the act of omission itself; and that [specification] is appropriately a statement of time. Therefore, it is not for the purpose of non-omission. (3)
The section concerning the performance of the Pavamāneṣṭis in a fire that has not been consecrated.
Sūtra: For those [offerings], Agni should be the archetype, as in the case of the Prayāja offerings. 19.
(Prima facie view) ||
There are the Pavamāna-iṣṭis, beginning with "To Agni Pavamāna," and so forth.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: should the Pavamāna-iṣṭis be performed in a fire consecrated by the Pavamāna-iṣṭis, or not? What is the prima facie view? Indeed, regarding those Pavamāna-iṣṭis...

The fires should be understood as being consecrated by the Pavamāna-iṣṭis. Why? Because of the force of the extended injunction (codaka), just like the Prayājas; for as it is said, "the Prayājas occur by virtue of the extended injunction," so too the fires should be consecrated by the Pavamāna-iṣṭis.
Sūtra: Or rather, it is not so, because they are for that purpose. (Conclusion) || 20 ||
Bhāṣya: Or rather, there should be no refinement of the fires by means of the Pavamāna-iṣṭis. Why?
Because there is no [textual basis] stating that it "should be established" (acit syāt).
--- Page 425 --- Chapter 3, Section 6 ||
Bhāṣya: Because they serve that purpose; it has been stated that those Pavamāna-iṣṭis are for the purpose of consecrating the fires (agni-saṃskāra).

And whatever is indeed an auxiliary (aṅga) is grasped by the extended application (codaka); however, these consecrations are prompted by the fire, not prompted by the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; therefore, they are not included by the codaka.

Moreover, the Pavamāna-iṣṭis apply to the archetype (prakṛti) which is devoid of the sacrificial refinements (iṣṭi-saṃskāra), because at that stage the Pavamāna-iṣṭis themselves have not yet been prescribed. (3.6.50)
The section concerning the fact that the *upākaraṇa*, *kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā-prasana*, and other rites belong to the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice.
Sūtra: The ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice applies to all [the deities] equally, because there is no distinction in the context.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, as stated: "When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. Likewise, there are the Savanīya and the Anubandhya animals.
And there are the ritual duties pertaining to the animals: from the *upākaraṇa* (dedication) to the *upānayanam* (bringing forward), the binding with a rope, and the boiling in broth.
Yoking, immolating, slaughtering—and so forth—are these [rites] for all [the animals], namely the Agniṣomīya, the Savanīya, and the Anūbandhya; or for the Agniṣomīya and the Savanīya;
or for the Agniṣomīya alone? What is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)?

Because there is no distinction among all the sacrificial animals. How is there no distinction? All the sacrificial animals are mentioned within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice; since they are established within that context, all the ritual duties pertaining to the animal sacrifice are connected to them, and there is no specific distinction made between them therein.

This being the case, we reply: these ritual properties (dharmas) should belong to the Savanīya [animal sacrifice]; the procedure for the animal sacrifice would be common to all, were there no distinction within the context (prakaraṇa). However, there is indeed a distinction within the context, for the animal properties are recited specifically in the context of the Savanīyas.
—“An animal dedicated to Agni is to be offered at the Uṣṭra-stoma; for on the following day, an animal dedicated to Indra is to be offered at the Ukthya, for the Ukthyas belong to Indra.
A ram dedicated to Indra is to be offered at the Ṣoḍaśin; for the ram is indeed dedicated to Indra, and it belongs to Indra.”
The *ṣoḍaśī*. At the *atirātra*, a ewe sacred to Sarasvatī is to be sacrificed; [she is] to be addressed as Sarasvatī.

In the Mīmāṃsā system (Bhāṣya): Since the characteristics of the animal sacrifice have been prescribed by way of introduction, they must therefore apply to the Savanīya [animal] because of the context.
Sūtra: And because of the position [of the word], it belongs to the preceding [section]. (2nd Pūrvapakṣa)
As for what was stated—that "because of the context, they are for the sake of the Savanīya"—this belongs to the Gulma school;
however, according to the sequence, they belong to the Agnīṣomīya, for it is recited in its sequence on the Upavasatha day. Therefore, they belong to both.
Sūtra: According to some, [the rule applies] even when one is away from home; and that [mention] is prior to the hearing [of the rule], being for the sake of a subordinate quality. (Siddhānta) 20.

According to some reciters of the Vedic branches (*śākhins*), there is a scriptural injunction for the *pravarasavanīya* offerings; with reference to that, this repeated scriptural mention is for the purpose of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*). [Question: "But what is the subordinate quality for the sake of which this scripture exists?
It is said: "For the attainment of cattle (*paśu-sannatyai*); just as a fish, when placed upon dry land, tosses about."

"Thus, indeed, these [fires], when not properly understood, shake the people"—having thus stated the fault in their lack of comprehension, the quality of the *vapāpracāra* (the offering of the omentum) is enjoined by means of the interrogative form: "How, O Agni, are the animal sacrifices possessed of animals? This scriptural passage (*śruti*) is for that purpose; it concerns the *vapā*—

Because they form a single syntactical unit through their sequential performance. What follows from this? If that is so, it is not the case that the animal-ritual details (*paśudharma*) belong to the *savanīya* offerings by virtue of context (*prakaraṇa*), but rather, by virtue of sequence (*krama*), they belong specifically to the *agnīṣomīya*. But what is that scriptural statement of sequence? "Having taken the *āśvina* cup, [one proceeds] with the *viṣṭuti*..."
"Having encircled the sacrificial post, he dedicates the animal for the Savanīya sacrifice to Agni."—thus [it is said].
Sūtra: If it is argued that this is a rule regarding time for the superior [rite]. (Ābhāsa 21)
Bhāṣya: This is not so—that [the offering] is for the sake of the Agniṣomīya alone by virtue of sequence; rather, because of the context (prakaraṇa), it is for the sake of the Savanīya.

The prior mention is for the purpose of enjoining it, while the ninefold vessel for the Āśvina [cup] is for the purpose of enjoining the time as a subordinate quality. How so? By that, the time for the [Savanīya] which has been postponed is indicated by the procedure involving the omentum (vapā).

This is prescribed: when the procedure for offering the omentum (*vapā*) at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) has been enjoined, the time for the immolation (*ālambha*) also follows thereat. Since no specific time would otherwise be fixed, the measure of time is prescribed by the rule: "Having taken the *āśvina* cup. [The text continues: "Having praised with the *viṣṭuti*, [one approaches] the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)."
--- Page 427 --- Chapter 1, Section 6 || 375 Bhāṣya:
"Having girt [the sacrificial post], he performs the *upākaraṇa*"; this is a restatement (*anuvāda*). For otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the general rule (*paribhāṣā*).

The time would have to be prescribed, as well as the bringing forward [of the animal]; thus, because of the prescription of multiple attributes, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda). Therefore, the characteristics of the animal pertain to the Savanīya sacrifice.
Sūtra: Not so, because it is a part [of the whole]. (Ābhāsvara-nirṇaya) 22.

Bhāṣya: This is not so. These [passages] refer sequentially to the meaning of the *ādya-uṣman* (the first heat); for the recitation at the time of the Āśvina cup is for the purpose of an injunction. If this were for the purpose of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), the sentence would be split; but it is not for the purpose of an injunction. Indeed, for that which has been displaced by the performance of the omentum (*vapā-pracāra*), a purpose regarding time is not possible.

For a single part is indeed a subsidiary of the omentum; therefore, because the preparatory rite (*upākaraṇa*) is a subordinate act (*sannipātī*) intended for the consecration of the omentum, it must be deferred [along with the omentum].
Sūtra: If it is argued that [the cognition] is due to the object. (Objection)

The Bhāṣya says: "In that case, the time for that which is superior [to the preceding] would be enjoined by the purpose. For it is heard in scripture: 'Having covered [the wound] with his fist, he should remain seated until the offering of the omentum (vapā). By the previous [method], having struck with the fist, one would not be able to remain seated for such a long time while covering [it] with the fist."
For the sake of attaining renown, his food, conduct, and other activities must be performed by him in such a way as to be blameless.
Sūtra: Not so, because of the prohibition in the Śruti. (Ābhāsasiddhānta)

Bhāṣya: This is not so. There would indeed be a contradiction with the Vedic texts if it were thus; however, there is no contradiction with the Vedic texts, for [the act] will be performed by covering [it] with a silent fist or a leaf-fist. [Objection: "But does the word *āste* (he sits) not occur in the sense of sitting? [Reply: Not necessarily only in the sense of sitting; it also occurs in the sense of remaining indifferent (*audāsīnya*).

It is also seen [used] in the sense of "remaining stationary," as in "he remains having taken hold of shrubs" or "he remains having taken hold of creepers"— thus it occurs even where there is no sitting down, namely, in the cessation of activity.
Here too, [the meaning is] "having covered [it] with a silent handful or a handful of leaves until the offering of the omentum (vapā)."

It will be recited [later]. Therefore, the mention of the time for the Āśvina cup is for the purpose of an injunction; the characteristics of the animal sacrifice do not belong to the context of the Savanīya offerings. Consequently, they are not for the sake of the Savanīyas.
--- Page 428 --- 376 Mīmāṃsā-darśana (The Inquiry into Vedic Exegesis)
Sūtra: Because of the position [of the mantra], it belongs to the preceding preparatory rite (saṃskāra), since its purpose is for that. 25.
(Upadeśa)

There is no *prakaraṇa* (contextual setting) for the *savanīya* offerings; this being the case, by the previously stated reason of *sthāna* (position), [the rite] must belong to the preceding *agnīṣomīya*. This refinement (*saṃskāra*) is connected with the animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*), not with the *jyotiṣṭoma*; for if it were connected with the *jyotiṣṭoma*, [it would not be so].

There would be a distinction regarding the animals; for even the animal sacrifices are capable of enjoining ritual duties because they possess an unprecedented character (*apūrva*) and are provided with a specific context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, by virtue of the sequence, the ritual details belong to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice.
Sūtra: And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (He0) || 26 ||

Bhāṣya: From this also we see that the animal-related rites are for the sake of the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice]. Why? Because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga). The indicative mark regarding the animal is as follows: "They proceed with the omentum at the morning pressing; with the sacrificial cake at the midday pressing. Thus, the animal...
He shows the *puroḍāśa* cake. Otherwise, if [the ritual] were of uniform application (*samānavidhāna*) across all animal sacrifices,
the *puroḍāśa*— being intended as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) for the two deities Agni and Soma— would, by virtue of its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*),
belong to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice and not to the *savanīya*, because those two [latter sacrifices] lack those two deities.
And it indicates this; therefore, they are for the sake of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice.
Sūtra: There is no injunction [of the mantra], because it serves the purpose of indicating a subordinate quality (guṇa). 27.

Bhāṣya: (This is a sūtra following the previous word. [The opponent] says: "But surely the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) is for the purpose of covering the openings [of the body], etc. We say: No. "Because it is not an injunction for the sake of an accessory" (na guṇārthena codanā); there is no injunction for the purpose of covering the openings; that is a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda)—this has already been stated. Therefore...

The purpose is for the consecration of the deity; therefore, since they serve the purpose of the Agniṣomīya [animal sacrifice], the observation of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) at the Savanīya is logically consistent, but not if they were common to both. Therefore, the characteristics of the animal sacrifice pertain specifically to the Agniṣomīya. (3.6.7)
--- Page 429 --- Chapter 3, Section 6 ||
The section concerning the nature of the duty of granting fearlessness and other such acts, such as the taking of branches.
Sūtra 370: Because of the difference in time between the two milkings, they should be combined. (Pūrvapakṣa)

There is the evening milking, and likewise there is the morning milking. However, there are certain properties of milking, such as the fetching of the branch, the driving forth of the cows, the stirring [of the milk], the milking of the cow, and so forth. Do these serve the purpose of the evening milking alone, or do they serve the purpose of both?
Thus [it is asked]. What, then, is the prima facie view?—The property belonging to those two milkings is independent.

Why? Because on the day of the *aupavasatha*, which is the sequence for the evening milking, they prescribe the fetching of the branches and so forth; and it is on that very same day that the evening milking takes place.
Therefore, by this sequence, the rules for milking apply to the evening milking.
Sūtra: Or rather, because of the context or because of the distinction, the scriptural injunction regarding time applies to that which is connected with it.
29 || (Siddhānta) ||

Commentary: For the context (*prakaraṇa*) is common to both; just as it applies to the curd, so it applies to the milk. And since context is stronger than sequence (*krama*), therefore the properties of the *doha* (milking) pertain to the purpose of both. Furthermore, the recitation of the evening milking does not take place on the preceding day; when then? On the following day. How so?

Thus they say: "The curds for Indra on the new-moon day; the milk for Indra on the new-moon day. For on the new-moon day, both [offerings] together with their constituent parts are enjoined. This very [milk-offering], which is for the sake of the evening milking, is performed on the preceding day; such is the inherent nature of the curds.

That which was commenced on the previous day is completed on the following day; therefore, the rules for milking are prescribed in the sequence of the evening milking. This being so, the very premise—that the properties of milking apply to both [the morning and evening milkings]—is not established. (3.6.8 Praśna)
The section concerning the fact that the *sāṃdana* and other [offerings] possess the characteristics of the three pressings (*savana*).
Sūtra: Likewise, there is no naming of the cups during the other pressings.
Commentary: There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma.
(Page 430)
Thus it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the Mīmāṃsā-Śāstra. In that regard, ten cups for Indra and Vāyu (aindravāyava) are prescribed for the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana).
And these ritual acts (dharmas) are heard [in the scripture]: "The cups (grahas) are set down at the Upāṃśu-savana; they are fixed at the Anūpaśu;
the cup is wiped with the *daśāpavitra*. There are other cups at the Mādhyandina-savana and others at the Tṛtīya-savana; regarding those [cups] belonging to the Mādhyandina and the Tṛtīya savanas...

And there is a doubt regarding the pressings (*savanas*): "Should the duties of the cups (*graha-dharma*) be performed for all [the cups], or only for those cups that are at the morning pressing (*prātaḥ-savana*)? What is the prima facie view? They should apply to the cups of the morning pressing; because they are recited in sequence with them, not with the others.

This being the case, we reply: the mention of the cups (*graha*) at the *mārjālīya* altar during the morning pressing and at the third pressing must pertain to those [pressings] alone. For the context (*prakaraṇa*) is equal for all of them, provided these ritual details (*dharma*) are recited; they are connected to the cup-offering by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*).
They are prescribed; and since sentence and context are stronger than order, therefore the properties of the cup-bearer (graha-dharma) apply to all [the cups]. (3.6.8) Thus ends the eighth section.
The section concerning the fact that the nature of all sacrificial animals applies to the chariot, the *nāñcī*, and so forth.
Sūtra: And there is [divine] composition, because of the observation of indicative marks. (32)
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the Agniṣomīya animal, as it is stated:

"The initiated one who sacrifices the Agniṣomīya animal. Regarding that, a construction is prescribed, and the properties of that construction are heard: "It should be made of reeds, it should be made of Darbha grass, and it should be placed upon the Prastara."

And thus there arises a doubt: "Are these properties common to both the arrangement of the Agniṣomīya and the arrangement of the Savanīya, or do they belong to the arrangement of the Agniṣomīya alone?
What is the prima facie view? [They belong] to the arrangement of the Agniṣomīya because of the context (prakaraṇa).
Thus it being the case, we reply: it is common to both. Why?
Because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*). There is an indicative mark; for thus it says: "Fire is the bond..."
"Having made the victim a bush, having sprinkled it with water, and having girt it with the cord, one should cook the animal dedicated to Agni"—
thus [it is said]. End of Chapter 3, Section 6.

In the section on the transformation of the girdle during the wearing of the garment (bhā. vasanīryapariṇyāṇe), the text shows the girdle; this demonstration is appropriate if it is common [to all]. If it belonged specifically to the animal sacrifice for Agni and Soma (agnīṣomīya), then it would not apply to the original [archetypal] rite.

One should turn back from the covering of the *savanīya* [animal]; for another covering is obtained for the *savanīya*, wherein variegation is observed. How so? "Having taken the cup for the Aśvins and gone out, he covers the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)"—thus it is said. In that case, if...

The girdle is not common [to both], for it would follow that the covering with cloth is required; however, the text indicates the girdle. Therefore, the girdle is common, and because of its commonality, that which belongs to it is also common. This commonality of the girdle is established by this indicative mark (*liṅga*). What is it here?

Is this indeed the correct principle? It is said: by virtue of the context, it belongs to the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice]; by virtue of the syntactical connection, it belongs to the measuring of the sacrificial post. (3.6.10)
The section concerning the fact that even the subsidiary parts possess ritual properties such as being placed on the altar and so forth.
Aṃ. 1: That which is left over from afar is not connected with others because of proximity. || 32 ||
(Verse)

Bhāṣya: Regarding that which remains distant from the Jyotiṣṭoma, such as the *śrauṣaṭ* and the *anuvākyā* sections which are recorded as being accompanied by mantras—therein arises a doubt: should the duties pertaining to the cups (*graha*) included within the Jyotiṣṭoma be performed, or not? What is the prima facie view? They should not be performed.

Because of non-proximity; for when it is stated, "He mixes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk," the cooking belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa alone and not to all [cups], so too this collection of ritual properties (dharmajāta) pertains only to what stands within the context (prakaraṇa), and not to all.
Or rather, it is connected [to the primary act], because the subsidiary is for the sake of that [primary] and is dependent upon it.
33 || (Siddhānta) ||

Bhāṣya: Or it may be connected with the dharmas; such would be its nature, even if it stands outside the context. Why? Because the syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than the context (*prakaraṇa*). [Objection: But surely there is another—Page 432—[favorable]...
In the Mīmāṃsā system, [it might be argued that] the *bhāṣā* mantras would not benefit the Jyotiṣṭoma. It is replied: they will indeed benefit it;
because, in the case of both the *saṃvāda* and *anumantraṇa*, this remnant is for the sake of that [Jyotiṣṭoma]. (That is, because it is for the purpose of the Jyotiṣṭoma.)
The property of the cup (*grahadharma*) is caused by the cup and serves as an auxiliary to the *Jyotiṣṭoma*;

therefore, it ought to apply to every cup that assists the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. Consequently, the property of the cup must be performed for both the *saṃvada* and the *āgrayaṇa* cups. Thus [it is concluded].
Sūtra: One should not persist in what has been refuted. (Aphorism 34, Adhikaraṇa 2, Section 1)

Bhāṣya: As for what was stated—namely, that "one mixes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk"—that is appropriate because of the direct scriptural statement regarding the mixing (*śravaṇa*); there, the specific restriction prevails by setting aside the general context (*prakaraṇa*). But here the case is the opposite:
in that instance, the context applies to all cups, while the sentence (*vākya*) applies to the specific ones; however, here [the context applies] to all cups.

The sentence [is the authority] for specific cases; the context [is the authority] for those within a specific section. Therefore, the ritual properties apply even to that which is not situated within a specific context—thus [it is concluded]. (3.3.129a)
