In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the initiations (*dīkṣā*) are heard in the text: "There are three initiations"; likewise, the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are heard: "Its sacrificial fee is one hundred and twelve. Regarding this, there is a doubt: are the initiation and the sacrificial fee for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the principal, or only for the principal?

[The opponent asks: "What is the prima facie view?"—namely, that because the men are for the purpose of both the subsidiary and the principal acts, the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) are for the purpose of both the subsidiary and the principal. This being the prima facie view, we reply:
the initiation and the sacrificial fee belong to the principal. Why? Because of the scriptural statement; for there is indeed a scriptural statement.
"— 'The initiations belong to Soma, the sacrificial fees belong to Soma'— for there is no [contradiction] of the scriptural statement.
In the Mīmāṃsā system, there is a section called the Śrutibhāra. Therefore, because of the observation of the initiation (dīkṣā) and because of the scriptural statement regarding Soma— so it is said.
Sūtra: And because of the observation of harshness. (12) (Yukti)

The Bhāṣya shows the *niṣṭhuti* in the context of initiation (*dīkṣā*). How so? "That which you requested with an animal, O Brahman—what is his initiation?"—"When he offers the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* oblation, that is his initiation. This statement occurs even though there is no [other] initiation present.
Therefore, there is the observation of the initiation of women—thus [it is concluded]. (3.7.5 pra.)
The section concerning the bending down within the sacrificial altar (antarvedi).
Sūtra: Likewise, the altar belongs to the sacrificial post. (Pūrvapakṣa)

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, as it is said: "When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. Regarding that, having driven in the sacrificial post (yūpa), it is heard:
"The sacrificial post is indeed a thunderbolt; if one were to fix it within the altar, it would burn [the sacrificer]; if outside the altar—"

"It should have nine points; one should fix it within the altar (antarvedi), and the base (śraddha) outside the altar (bahirvedi); it becomes 'not having points below' (avachṛṅkha), so that it does not burn [the ground].
Regarding this, there is a doubt: when it says "within the altar," does the altar refer to the sacrificial ground upon which the sacrificial post (yūpa) stands?

Is it taught [as a rule], or is it stated for the purpose of defining a location—namely, "inside the altar" (*antarvedi*) or "outside the altar" (*bahirvedi*)? How is it an auxiliary part of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), or how is it a definition of location? If there were a connection between the auxiliary part of the post and the interior of the altar...
It is intended that the sacrificial post (yūpa) must be constructed as connected to the altar (vedi); therefore, it is by way of its being attached to the post.
Alternatively, that location where half of the post being measured lies within the edge of the altar and half lies outside is indicated;
thus, it is a definition by way of location (deśalakṣaṇā).
What is established?— "In the same way as the altar belongs to the sacrificial post," just as the initiation and the sacrificial fees belong to the principal rite,
so the altar belongs to the sacrificial post; in the same way the sacrificial post is to be measured, and in the same way it is being measured.

The altar (vedi) exists within the middle part of the sacrificial ground (aṅga). In this way, the scriptural mention of the "altar" will also be upheld; otherwise, the word "altar" would indicate a location through secondary implication (lakṣaṇā). Between direct statement (śruti) and its indication, the direct statement is the explanation, not the indication. Therefore, the altar is designated as a constituent part (aṅga) of the sacrificial post (yūpa).
Sūtra: Or rather, it is merely a location, because it forms a single syntactical unit with the [preceding] injunction. (Siddhānta) || 14 ||

The Bhāṣya [states]: "Or rather, only the location is indicated by the word 'vedī' (altar), not the physical component of the altar itself. Why? Because of its syntactical unity with the sentence regarding the fire-altar: 'He fixes one part within the altar and another part outside the altar. This syntactical unity with that [injunction] must be maintained if there is an indication of location; otherwise,"

The altar (vedi) is mentioned as being an auxiliary part of the sacrificial post (yūpa); therefore, its mention outside the altar is not to be enjoined. When the altar is taught as an auxiliary to the sacrificial post, the notion that "the auxiliary is outside the altar" does not arise in any way to serve a useful purpose.

‘Now, if one were to enjoin the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) outside the altar (*vedī*) as being a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the post, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Therefore, if the altar is mentioned as having the sacrificial post as its subordinate part, the word “outside the altar” must by no means be enjoined. However, if it is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a location, then [the injunction applies] to that specific [location].’

When the location is being specified, the word "outside the altar" (bahirvedi) must necessarily be supplied; for if it were not mentioned, it would be understood that the sacrificial post (yūpa) could be placed in any location whatsoever, either within the middle of the altar or elsewhere. However, when the word "outside the altar" is actually heard, it is understood to be a subordinate factor (aṅga) pertaining to whichever specific location the post is being measured.

"A limb [of the sacrificial post] is inside the altar and [another] outside the altar; that location is intended to be indicated, and it cannot be indicated without the word 'outside the altar' (bahirvedi)—thus, it must necessarily be taught. Therefore, this is an indication of a location. (3.7)
The section concerning the fact that the *havirdhāna* is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *sāmidhenī* verses.
Sūtra: [The term] "sāmidhenī" is applied because of the statement regarding the two *havirdhāna* carts, "They call it that which resembles the *sāmidhenīs*" (15). (Pūrvapakṣa)
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard: "And that which they press [the Soma], one should recite the Sāmidhenī verses after that...
— Page 446 — [text continues]
In the Mīmāṃsā system (Bhāṣya):
"Thus, they press [the Soma] with the Havirdhāna [cart] at the Havirdhāna [sheds]; that [is] the sāmi-..."

The meaning is that [the term] should be connected with the *sāmidhenīs*. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the *havirdhāna* enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *sāmidhenīs*, such that the *sāmidhenīs* qualified by the *havirdhāna* are to be recited; or rather, is it that the *sāmidhenīs* being recited are [qualified] by the *havirdhāna*?
Is an injunction perceived? What, then, is the prima facie view? The *havirdhāna* (the oblation-holding cart) is enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *sāmidhenī* verses;
that *havirdhāna* in which they press the Soma is to be connected with the *sāmidhenīs*. Therefore, the *sāmidhenīs* are connected to the *havirdhāna*.

Because of the statement, "The dhenu-cows are to be recited after [the Sāmidhenīs]," the scriptural mention of the Havirdhāna shed will be supported when it functions as a subordinate part of the Sāmidhenīs; otherwise, it would have to be indicated by secondary implication (lakṣaṇā).
Therefore, the name 'Havirdhāna' is a subordinate part of the Sāmidhenīs.
Sūtra: Or rather, the direct perception [of the Soma] pertains only to its location, because it is the action of the substance. (16) (Conclusion)

Bhāṣya: Furthermore, this is stated for the sake of location—that is, "in whichever place they press [the Soma], in that place the *sāmidhenī* verses are to be recited"—for by that, a visible purposeful act (*arthakarma*) is performed for the Soma;
namely, "the southern *havirdhāna* cart is for the purpose of placing the Soma."

First, this [Soma] is to be taken up for the purpose of placing the Soma; likewise, the *sāmidhenī* verses are also to be taken up for the purpose of kindling the fire. However, in this context, it is heard as follows:
"The *sāmidhenīs* connected to that *havirdhāna* cart near which they press the Soma [are to be recited] for the fire..."

"They are to be adopted for the purpose of kindling"—this being the case, it is not known whether the *sāmidhenī* verses assist the *havirdhāna* cart, or whether the *havirdhāna* cart assists the *sāmidhenīs*. To this it is replied: first of all, the *sāmidhenīs* do not [assist] the *havirdhāna*.
They provide assistance; for it is not yet enjoined that "the sāmidhenīs are to be recited.
What then? Rather, their connection with the specific *havirdhāna* (grain-receptacle) is what is enjoined.

Between the two eastern openings of the two structures named Havirdhāna, which are situated on the southern and northern sides within the Havirdhāna pavilion, that which is on the south is designated by the term "dakṣiṇa" and that which is on the north by the word "uttara.
Near that [southern opening] is the pressing of the Soma. Mādhava maintains that the word "ut" here functions in the sense of the prefix "apa," meaning "eastward."
--- Page 447 --- Chapter 3, Section 7 ||
There are 365 [verses].
Nor is there an unordained *ṛc*, nor is it ordained in this manner: "It should be taken up and connected by those following the *havirdhāna* cart. How so?
What then? The connection of the *sāmidhenī* verses with a specific *havirdhāna* [cart] is indicated;

the connection with the *havirdhāna* is what is enjoined. And no connection of the *sāmidhenīs* with the *havirdhāna* has been previously established, which would require one to adopt a specific instance. By what, then, is the *havirdhāna* connected?

For the function of the *soma* is directly perceived [in relation to the *havirdhāna*], whereas the function of the *sāmidhenī* verses is not directly perceived in relation to the *havirdhāna*. However, there is a connection between the *sāmidhenī* verses and a location; by the statement "to the west of the altar," the location of the *hotṛ* priest is indicated, and that [location] belongs either to the northern or the southern [of the two *havirdhāna* sheds].

The term *havirdhāna* is a designation; thus, the statement "they recite after that which they press" is appropriate. Therefore, the mention of *havirdhāna* is for the purpose of indicating a location.
[Objection: Why should the connection not be as follows: "in whichever *havirdhāna*..."?
“They press [the Soma]; this [act] has a connection with the *sāmidhenī* verses of that *havirdhāna* [shed]”—this cannot be so.
For if it were thus, two injunctions would have to be established:
a connection with the *havirdhāna* and a connection with a specific *havirdhāna*; and in that case, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, it is not so.
The connection is as follows.
Sūtra: And the designation is likewise [indicative]. (Yukti 17)
And the designation is exactly that; for example, as when it is taught regarding the two carts: "The Havirdhāna shed is for the sake of Soma. (3.7.7 Śrauta-sūtra).
The names of the limbs [are so called] because they are the substrata for other latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Sūtra: The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer, because that is its characteristic; therefore, it should apply to one's own performance. (Pūrvapakṣa)

Bhāṣya: Here, ritual acts (*karman*) are the examples—namely, "One desiring heaven should offer the *agnihotra*," "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*," and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *jyotiṣṭoma*. In this regard, there is a doubt: are these ritual acts [to be performed] by themselves...
--- Page 448 --- 566 In the Mīmāṃsā System of Philosophy.

[Commentary: Regarding those who perform [the rites], should one perform the *ṛc* oneself because of the injunction, while another performs the remainder or one may do so oneself; or must another alone perform the remainder? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It should be performed by oneself. Why? Because the fruit belongs to one who performs it oneself. How so?

How is it understood? "Because of its possession of that [quality]," meaning that sound is the indicator (lakṣaṇa) of this object; for one who employs it himself, there is a result. What is that sound? It is "one desiring heaven should sacrifice"; he who desires heaven is thus designated as the agent (kartā) in the sacrifice.
"One should accomplish the fruit through cultivation"—thus, the agent who performs it along with its constituent parts attains the fruit of cultivation;
therefore, it should be performed by oneself.

Sūtra: But in the case of the general rule, because of the predominance [of the principal], the performer of the subsidiary acts is like the performer of the principal; therefore, it may be either another person or oneself. (Pūrvapakṣa) 16.

In the case of the *utsarga* (the act of relinquishment), there is primacy. How so? He who performs the *utsarga* has thereby accomplished everything. How? The *parikraya* (hiring) is part of the *utsarga*; by means of it, all [the priests] are engaged and perform [their duties].
Therefore, he who performs the *parikraya* has himself accomplished everything.
Therefore, one should perform the renunciation (*utsarga*) oneself; as for the remainder, another may perform it or one may do so oneself.

Sūtra: Or it may be another [Self], because of the purchase [of the officiating priests] and because of the prohibition of [the sacrificer's own] eating and so forth; [this applies] with respect to the non-inner Self. (Siddhānta) 20.

[The opponent says: "The performer of the remaining [acts] must be someone else. Why? Because there is no scriptural injunction for hiring (parikraya). Among the many modes of employing persons, hiring is restricted [to specific cases].
Therefore, all ritual items (padārthas) must be performed by those who are not hired through payment. This is the opposing view.
The purchase [of services] is established as being for oneself. If one were to perform [the rites] oneself, it would be performed by one who has not been purchased;
and that would render the scriptural injunction regarding purchase meaningless, or else it would imply an invisible (transcendental) purpose.
Therefore, the remaining constituent acts must be performed by others who have been purchased.
But when one performs the relinquishment oneself, everything becomes performed by oneself. (3.7.8)
--- Page 449 --- Chapter 3, Section 7.
367. The section concerning the rule regarding the specific number of priests who have been hired.
Sūtra: And that [number] should be a single measure for different purposes; there is no fixed rule because there is no distinction. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 21 ||
And since those [priests] have been hired for that purpose, there would be no restriction on the number of performers regarding the duties to be performed.
Why? Because of the lack of specification; no specific rule regarding the number of performers is prescribed in the sacred texts.
Their number is determined by the purpose: as many as are required to accomplish the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) until the result is achieved, so many should be employed.
Choose!
Or rather, because of the difference in scriptural statements, there should be separate [deities] for each name. Sūtra 22.
Bhāṣya: As many ritual acts as are heard of by their names, so many [priests] are to be chosen;

they are distinguished by those hearings of their names—“The Pratiprasthātṛ divides the cake,” “The Pratiprasthātṛ offers the churning-oblation,” “The Neṣṭṛ leads the wife to sing the udgītha,” “The Unnetṛ...”.
"He draws up the cups"— likewise, "the Prastotṛ chants the Prastāva, the Udgātṛ sings the Udgītha, the Pratihartṛ chants the Pratihāra, the Subrahmaṇya recites the Subrahmaṇyā,
the Hotṛ recites the Prātaranuvāka, the Maitrāvaruṇa gives the directions and recites the responses."

The Acchāvāka performs the sacrifice, and the Grāvastut recites the Grāvastocīyā verses—this much is the purpose of these ritual acts; therefore, in their performance, these [priests] must necessarily be chosen as prescribed by the sacred texts. There are no ritual elements (padārtha) apart from these, even when considered through the application of syntactical connection (vākya).
It was not explicitly taught; it is understood through traditional designation (samākhyā). Therefore, one should choose this many.
Sūtra: If it is argued that [the rule applies] because of the difference in the actions of a single [person], (Prābhākara).
If it is thus proposed— "one should choose this many"— and therein it is intended that "whosoever shall perform that rite," then each such person is denoted by that term.
In the Mīmāṃsā system (Bhāṣya),
it is stated that even a single person may be told to perform many ritual acts, as in the case of one who is struck by a thunderbolt.
Therefore, there is no fixed rule.
Sūtra: For there is no production [of names].

(Ābhāsa-nirṇaya 24). Bhāṣya: This is not so. Regarding the production of persons, when there is an absence of specific means [for their distinction], the designations of persons indeed differ: "He chooses a Brāhmaṇa; he chooses a Hotṛ; he chooses an Udgātṛ..."

"He chooses the Tāra; he chooses the Adhvaryu"—and so forth. Therefore, there is a need for those who bear such names in the ritual; they must necessarily be chosen. Consequently, the mention of their choosing is not an injunction (*vidhi*), because there is no purpose [for it]; nor is it a restatement (*anuvāda*), because there is no [prior] basis for it.

One should not say, "So many [priests] are to be chosen according to the Veda," for that would be meaningless. And this [text] is intended to convey a specific distinction among them; therefore, this statement is for the purpose of making known that specific distinction which pertains to them. Consequently, there are sixteen performers.
They are to be chosen; furthermore, Soma would be the agent, and the same applies to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices as well.
The separate section concerning the Camasādhvaryus.
Sūtra: [The *camasādhvaryu*s are distinct] because they are designated by those [other priests]. (25)
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there are the Camasādhvaryus, as indicated by the injunction: "One should choose the Camasādhvaryus.
Regarding them, a doubt arises: are they some among these [previously mentioned priests], or are they others distinct from them?
What, then, is the prima facie view? Since they are enumerated among those very [priests], they must be some among them.
This being the position reached, we reply: the *camasādhvaryus* must be others than those [eight], distinct from them.
Why? Because of the designation by them; there is a designation by means of those eight who have been enumerated:
"The *camasādhvaryus* of the central performers, the *camasādhvaryus* of the *hotṛ*-class priests... and so forth.
“[They are] the *camasādhvaryus*”—so it is said.

[Objection: “But surely those who have already been dispatched as *adhvaryus* should themselves be the *camasādhvaryus*. [Reply: No, we say. Why? Because of the designation by them: “the *camasādhvaryus* of those who act from the middle.”
--- Page 451 --- Chapter 1, Section 7.
Regarding the statement "the Camasādhvaryus of the Hotrakas"—this genitive case occurs because there is a relationship [of ownership];

they are designated by the priests (*ṛtvij*), meaning the priests are their masters and not the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and it has been our established position that these are distinct from the sacrificer's attendants. It is not [the case that they belong to the sacrificer].
The Camasādhvaryus are to be chosen by the sacrificer to perform their duties; they are to be chosen by the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
Furthermore, there is a distinction regarding them even in their original injunction:
"Two Camasādhvaryus for each [cup]. (3.7.10)
The section concerning the rule regarding the plurality of the *camasādhvaryu* priests.
Sūtra: But at the time of origination, [the authority belongs] to one who has heard much. 26.

Regarding these very [camasādhvaryus], there is a doubt: is there no restriction—as to whether it is one, two, or many—or are there necessarily many? When the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that there is no restriction, it is replied: "There are many. Why? Because in the originative injunction, the plural is heard: "the camasādhvaryus. Thus, for them...
In the case of origination, there is great learning; therefore, there are many—thus [it is concluded]. (3.7.11)
The section concerning the rule that the number of *camasādhvaryu* priests is ten.
Sūtra: The number ten [is established] because of the observation of an indicative mark. 27.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there are the Camasādhvaryu priests, and it has been stated that they are many. When the doubt arises as to how many "many" there are, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that they are three, on the strength of the plural number. To this we reply: "Their number is ten, because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga)"; they should be ten, for such is the indicative mark.
In the Daśapeya, which is a modification of the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard: "Ten Camasādhvaryu priests, ten by ten, follow each cup; for this reason, it is called the Daśapeya.
By stating this, [the text] indicates ten Camasādhvaryu priests, provided that there are three...
If they were [only] three, this observation would not be possible. Therefore, this number exceeds three;
and if there were not ten, this observation would not be possible. Therefore— [Page 452] —
In the Mīmāṃsā system (Mīmāṃsā-darśana), there are eight hundred [units];
there are ten of these, and ten are their owners. Therefore, for the sake of the purpose—
The number ten is taken up, and when that is taken up, another number is also included; therefore, there would also be ten [of those]. (3|7|12 pra0)
The section concerning the agent of the act of smiling.
And [the word] *saṃśmitā* [is a separate term], because of the difference in sound. (Pūrvapakṣa 28)

The Bhāṣya states: There is a mention of the *śmitṛ* (the one who smiles), namely, "One should initiate the *śmitṛ*. Is he one among those already mentioned, or is he someone other than them? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Since he is mentioned in the context of their selection (*varaṇa*), he must be one among them. To this, it is replied:
"—And because of the difference in the word 'smṛta'. The word differs:

"This ritual is to be performed by one who has such-and-such a name"; therefore, one with such a name must be produced. Because of this mention, it is understood that [the performer] is qualified by a specific number; therefore, there should be another person designated as 'smṛta'.

Furthermore, there is the suspicion regarding one who is not a Brāhmaṇa, based on the statement: "One should give the Vikartana [portion] to the Komā to carry, and that to the Śamitṛ; if he should be a non-Brāhmaṇa, then to a Brāhmaṇa"—such a suspicion does not apply to the officiating priest (ṛtvij).
Sūtra: [The rule applies] because of the connection with the origin in the context and so forth. (Siddhānta) || 28 ||

[Commentary: It is true that [the number] is understood through qualifiers consisting of numbers, but not in the case of things that are being produced; rather, that non-production which is understood regarding them results from the distinction of actions for a single [entity]. This is also logically consistent. As for what was said—that there arises the suspicion that [it is] "not a Brāhmaṇa"—that refers to the intention of the sacrificer.

“If it should be a non-Brahmin who is the sacrificer”—[this is the objection]. [The opponent asks: “But surely, in the phrase ‘if it should be a non-Brahmin,’ the word *śmitā* (praise) is connected [to the non-Brahmin]? It is replied:
*Śmitā* means *śminā*; this is an etymological (*yaugika*) term used even for those things that are praiseworthy.
Because it is recited together with the *ṛc* verses, it must be performed by the *adhvaryu*;
since there is no purpose [for more], the number ten is not increased—this is the reading in the Kātyāyana-Śrautasūtra manuscript.
--- Page 453 --- 1. 2 Adhyāya, 7 Pāda ||
Commentary: Therefore, from that act of going, the sacrificer becomes fatigued; this being the case, the sacrificer who does not go [by proxy] remains connected [to the ritual]. (3.7.13) [Sūtra]
The suffixes *upagu*, *asṛj*, *adhikaraṇa*, and *ag* [are added to denote the agent].
Sūtra: [The soul is atomic] because of the observation of its going, coming, and so forth. (30)

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there are those known as the *santatopagās*. Because of the difference in their names, they convey an increase in the number [of participants]—namely, that they are distinct from the *arvā* and others.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: some of them must be among those very same [participants]. Why? Because they are enumerated within the group that has already arisen; for they are etymologically derived [from the same root].
And this is an indicative mark (liṅga) regarding the word "having made": "The Adhvaryu does not sing along.

If there were others besides these [the Prastotṛ, Udgātṛ, and Pratihartṛ], he would not prohibit the Adhvaryu, because [singing along) would not have been applicable to him. Since he prohibits it, we understand that it was mentioned at the point of origin (utpatti).
"Or one of the others"—thus [it is stated]. (3.7.14 Śrauta Sūtra)
The section concerning the distinctness of the seller of Soma.
Sūtra: But the seller is different [from the sacrificer], because the act [of selling] is not enjoined [for him]. (31)

In the Bhāṣya: There is a seller of Soma, and regarding him there is a doubt—is he one of the [officiating priests] such as the Adhvaryu and others, or is he someone other than them? What is the prima facie view? Since they are specifically mentioned, he must be one of them. To this we reply: "But the seller is another."
It might be argued: "The seller is not enjoined; rather, the purchase is enjoined. And that [purchase] is for the purpose of acquiring wealth and so forth.

Furthermore, it is for the sake of performing the constituent parts (*padārtha*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice that the Adhvaryu and other priests are produced [as required], but the sale of the Jyotiṣṭoma is not heard of in the scripture. Therefore, one does not address the Adhvaryu and others [with the call]."
"Darkness"—thus [it is said]. (3.7.15 Śrauta Sūtra)
In the Mīmāṃsā system,
the section concerning the universal applicability [of the *jyotiṣṭoma*] by means of the [term] *jyotiṣṭomatva*.
6. [The view that] all [are priests] because there is no distinction in their status as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) due to the performance of the ritual action. || 32 ||

(Prima facie view: Bhāṣya: Regarding these persons who are mentioned in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma, are they all officiating priests (ṛtvij), or only some among them? What is the prima facie position? All of them. Why?

‘From the performance of the ritual act,’ all perform the means of sacrifice; therefore, all seasons sacrifice. And those who perform the four [seasons] are the *ṛtvij*s (priests); no specific distinction is resorted to, such as “only these four perform [the sacrifice],” whereby they would be the *ṛtvij*s, while these others are not.
—Thus [it is said]. Therefore, all [the priests] possess the status of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

[Objection: But is it not the case that an exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*) is heard in the text: “There are seventeen officiating priests for the performer of the Soma sacrifice”? [Reply: It is said in response: In the case of an exclusive specification, many...
As for the statement "there are defects," this will be a restatement based on scriptural authority.
Sūtra: Or rather, it is not so, because of the restrictive enumeration. (Siddhānta)

[The Bhāṣya says: Or rather, not all [are included]. Why? Because of an enumeration; for it is heard in scripture: "There are seventeen priests for the Soma sacrifice performed by the sacrificer. This is not an injunction (*vidhi*), because a larger number is already established; nor is it a restatement (*anuvāda*), because it serves a purpose.

Sūtra: And austerity [is a means], because it is the accomplishment of results, as in the case of the world. (6)

Regarding austerity (tapas), it is heard in scripture: "One who performs [it] does not obtain what is difficult to traverse; one who does not perform [it] does not obtain food. In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the austerity pertaining to the officiating priest (ārtvija) or the sacrificer (yajamāna)? What is the prima facie view?
On account of the designation (samākhyāna), it follows that the austerity pertains to the officiating priest. Thus...
To this we reply: the austerity belongs to the sacrificer. Why? Because it is for the sake of accomplishing the fruit;

austerity is for the accomplishment of the fruit, and the fruit of the sacrifice is accomplished by one who has perfected the austerity. How is this understood? For austerity is suffering, and suffering is the fruit of unrighteousness (*adharma*), whereas the sacrifice is [a means of righteousness].

It becomes an obstacle to the fruit; for that [fruit] is conducive to the highest good (*śreyas*). Therefore, while it exists, the highest good cannot come to be; thus, it must be removed. Furthermore, merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are opposed by the enjoyment of the fruit. Therefore, it is taught in scripture that merit leads to the experience of the fruit of suffering. By means of that [merit],...

"Suffering is to be produced; this is that"—thus it becomes a matter of perceived reality, and one need not postulate an unperceived [result]. For the sacrifice, being bound by those factors impelled by the enjoyment of the fruit, will bestow the fruit; the accomplishment of the fruit for the sacrificer does not arise from his status as the agent.
Therefore, austerity belongs to the sacrificer. Thus it is said.

That which is separated must be understood as unseparated; however, this [unseparated state] is already established, for the connection with the presence of *brahmavarcasa* through the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) is directly perceived, and even the verbal suffix of the injunction is required for the birth [of the result].

The Bhāṣya says: "How will the mere injunctive suffix alone come from elsewhere [to be connected] with this verbal root-meaning such as *pratiṣṭhā* (establishment)? It is replied: It will exist together with the verbal root-meaning, not alone; therefore, there is no fault. Now...

Or rather, the injunctive suffix that occurs in connection with the nights will enjoin this specific result such as "firm foundation" (pratiṣṭhā) through the performance-injunction (prayogavacana), or it will serve as a commendatory statement (stuti) together with those results like "firm foundation. Bhāṣya: Now, as for what was said—that just as in such passages as "He whose *sruva* ladle is made of *khadira* wood," the mention of a fruit is an *arthavāda*, so it might be here as well—it is appropriate that there the mention of a fruit is an *arthavāda*, because a direct injunction of a fruit is impossible; [therefore, it is] an *arthavāda* regarding the fruit.

And because it is possible [to explain it otherwise]. As it has been said: "In the case of substances, purificatory acts, and rituals, since they are for the sake of another, the mention of a fruit must be an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda)" (Sūtra 4.3.1). (Śabara-bhāṣya 4.3.8)

The optional rites (*kāmyāni karmāṇi*) are the examples—for instance, "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya"—and so forth. In this regard, there is a doubt:
is heaven the desired fruit of these rites, or is the specific desire itself the fruit? What is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)?

"In the case of an optional rite (*kāmya-karman*), heaven (*svarga*) would be the permanent result. How so? A general term denoting all human goals is not restricted to a specific [result], for its connection with the visible word "desirer of heaven" (*svargakāma*) is indeed possible. He says:
"But is it not the case that a qualifying word is heard—namely, 'one desiring Brahman-splendor' (*brahmavarcasakāma*)? This is not a qualifier;

rather, this is a statement of a condition (*upādhi*). It is just as when someone who has set out to fetch firewood is told, "You must also bring a gourd"—this is merely an addition to the task of fetching firewood.

A second [act] is enjoined in proximity to the authority for the fetching of wood, such that:

"One should accomplish the carrying forward [of the water] by means of the *hanana* for one desiring cattle"— that is to say, "he who desires cattle should accomplish the carrying forward by means of the *godohana* [vessel]."

Sūtra: And when the cause has ceased, because of the restriction. "One should employ [the rite], or if it does not rain, one should employ it when dawn has broken"—
if heaven were not [the result], for what purpose would there be this restrictive rule? Therefore, heaven is eternal.

Bhāṣya: Or rather, the result would be desire (*kāma*), not heaven; for its injunction occurs through connection with that [desire], not through connection with the "desire for heaven" (*svargakāma*). Furthermore, there is an absence of a single syntactical unity even with the inferred [word] "desire for heaven"; however, there is a direct perception [of the word] through the expression of desire. And direct perception is more authoritative than inference.
Therefore, desire alone is the fruit.
Sūtra: [The subsidiary] is for the sake of the limb, because it is a quality.

(Ābhāsaniyama 9) Bhāṣya: Now, as for what was said—"just as in the case of the subsidiary of the sacrifice"—that is correct, "because it is for the sake of the limb. For there is a direct connection with the ritual (*kratu*) and with the desire—"he who may be desirous of cattle..."
"He should accomplish the carrying forward [of the water] by means of the milking vessel"— thus it is said; however,
there is no direct scriptural statement here to the effect that "he who desires spiritual luster should [perform] the sacrifice."
In the Mīmāṃsā system (Bhāṣya): [the sacrifice] would bring about heaven. How then? One who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
It might be that he should accomplish it by means of that sacrifice; therefore, it cannot be like a subsidiary (aṅga). Thus.
Sūtra: And when [the fire] has been extinguished, it is for the sake of the restrictive rule. (A0 Ni0 2)

[Commentary: Now, as for what was said—that when the desire for the fruit has ceased, or when the fruit has been obtained, a rule of completion is observed—we do not say that. [Rather,] the rule applies when it has ceased for that purpose;
the rule exists when it has ceased, and likewise for both purposes. For what? To avoid the censure of the learned.
If one undertakes [a rite] but does not complete it, the learned (śiṣṭas) would immediately censure him,
saying, "This performer is a base man. For the learned censure those who, having intended an oblation for the gods, do not bring the sacrifice to completion.
Therefore, it must necessarily be completed; in that case, this view will be logical:
"If it should rain, one should offer only that much. Consequently, for optional rites, the desire itself is the fruit. (4.3.8)
The section concerning the fact that the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices serve the purpose of fulfilling all desires.

Sūtra: That [rite] indeed is for the sake of desired results, because of the desire for the subsidiaries, on account of the context. (Pūrvapakṣa)

Bhāṣya: This is stated [in the scripture]: "Other sacrifices are performed for the sake of a single desire, whereas the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are for the sake of all [desires]; other rituals are undertaken for the sake of a single desire, whereas the Jyotiṣṭoma is for the sake of all [desires]. In this regard, there is a doubt: what...?

Regarding the phrase *aṅgakāmaḥ aṅga*: Is this a restatement (*anuvāda*) together with the *aṅgakāmas*, or is it an injunction (*vidhi*)? What is the prima facie view? It is a restatement; that which is "desirable for all" (*sarvakāmya*) is here being restated. Together with the *aṅgakāmas*—for indeed, there are *aṅgas*.
And desires, O dear one, as well as desires for specific results; for example: "For one desiring cattle, the cake for Agni...

"One should construct the altar with dug-out earth for one desiring a firm foundation"— thus [the texts] teach regarding the altar and so forth;
likewise, "If he should desire, 'May Parjanya rain,'" [they teach], but they do not say this regarding the *sadas*.
Regarding the phrase "minuyāt," we consider it proper that this is a restatement (anuvāda), since this very act has already been enjoined.
Sūtra: Or rather, it is an instruction regarding the fruit, because of the employment of the principal term. (26)

[The opponent says: It is for the sake of obtaining the fruit. Why? Because the connection with the fruit occurs through the word denoting the primary [rite], as in "the Darśapūrṇamāsa for all [desires]" and "the Jyotiṣṭoma for all [desires]";
and by the mention of the primary rite, its possession of all fruits is enjoined. Therefore...

Nor is it a restatement (*anuvāda*). If it were to depend upon the desires for the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the desires for the sub-subsidaries (*aṅgāṅga*), then there would be a case of indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*); and direct audition (*śruti*) is more authoritative than indirect indication. Therefore, the injunction is by means of the *prayogavacana* (the statement of performance). (4.3.10 Śrauta-sūtra)
The section concerning the separate performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites for each respective fruit.
(The Principle of the Accomplishment of Yoga)
Sūtra: And that [is established] because of the exclusion of all particulars. (Pūrvapakṣa) 27.

Bhāṣya: It has been stated regarding examples of this kind that "the injunction for all desires applies to the primary act. Now, the following is considered: do all desires [fulfilled] in a single performance, or by way of alternation? What is the prima facie view?
"If performed once, all desires [are attained]"—how so? Because both the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and the Jyotiṣṭoma are the occasion (nimitta) for all desires;
and if they are the occasion for all desires, what desire indeed would not be fulfilled?
Therefore, all desires [are attained] simultaneously.

Sūtra: Or rather, there is the accomplishment of yoga, because the object is useful. (Siddhānta)

Bhāṣya: This is not the case—that all desires [are fulfilled] simultaneously; rather, there is "attainment through yoga" (yoga-siddhi) in succession, and thus the desires would arise in succession. Why? Because "due to the non-simultaneity of their arising," these objects called desires do not all arise at once.

They arise; however, there is no possibility of all [the desires] arising simultaneously because of contradiction. Alternatively, regarding the phrase "because of not being connected with arising"—this is not a statement about the arising of the desires themselves, but rather a statement concerning them as characteristics of those [desires] that have already arisen, from which all desires [are fulfilled] by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

And [the case of] the Jyotiṣṭoma is likewise; it is not that all desires are remembered as resulting from ritual action, for ritual action is enjoined only for those [specific] desires which are [so specified]. Or thus:
[the next section] is the discussion concerning the fact that optional rites possess fruits both in this world and in the hereafter.
Sūtra: And that [belongs] to all, because there is no distinction. (Pūrvapakṣa)

Desirable rites (*kāmyāni karmāṇi*) serve as examples: "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a pap (*caru*) to Sūrya; one desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds (*ekādaśakapāla*) to Indra and Agni;
one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *Citrā*; one desiring a village should offer the *Sāṅgrahaṇī* to the Viśvedevas. (*sāṅgrahyāṇī* is a variant of *sāṅgrahaṇī*).

—Thus, there is a doubt regarding them: are these desires in this world, or rather in that world? What is the prima facie view? That the desires are in "that" (world), because there is no distinction; for just as heaven is [in that world], so too are these, since they have not been mentioned immediately after [the mention of that world].

The fruit of an action is perceived later; and that which is perceived immediately after [the action] is understood to arise from it—just as at whatever time the threshing occurs, at that same time the *sāṅgrahṇī* (winnowing) [occurs]. (*Note: This reading is found in the Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series edition.*)
Chapter 4, Section 3. Page 561.
507 bhā. Pleasure; and as for that which is perceived at a later time, its cause is likewise directly perceived to be something else entirely.
However, there is no cause whatsoever for the assumption of a body other than the unseen force (adṛṣṭa). Therefore...

It should be understood that the fruit consisting of a distinguished sense-faculty, body, and so forth, arises from a karma that possesses five fruits and is capable of bringing about union with that [result]. For this is shown: "Kauṣtuka, desiring to know, said to Dālbhya: 'By this [verse], one should lead me to the kingdom.'"
"Perform the sacrifice for me," [the king] said; he [the priest] replied, "O gentle one, you do not know that the kingdom must be protected;
sacrifices are undertaken for the sake of such desires"—thus he shows that [sacrifices] have fruits in another birth. Therefore, optional rites have fruits in another birth.
Sūtra: And there is the attainment of yoga because of the absence of connection with birth. 28.
(Sūtra) ||
Bhāṣya: Here indeed is the accomplishment of this yoga; it is not that a yogin does not exist by virtue of its arising.
He who sees and desires may perform [the practice] by means of this yoga. Nor is it understood from this that [its accomplishment] is impossible in this very life. And as for what was said...

"—is not perceived immediately thereafter"—this is the point. It is not known through perception or inference, but there is comprehension through verbal testimony (*śabda*). As for the objection that "at another time there will be another cause," this is not a fault; there may be another [cause], and this [present one] as well. And as for that which...
—“Sacrifices are brought for such-and-such a desire”—to this it is replied:

he should be addressed thus: “I will not cause you to sacrifice with that which has its fruit here, but I will cause you to sacrifice with that which has its fruit in the hereafter. Therefore, this [is the case].
This has been refuted—thus [it is concluded]. (Sūtra 3.3.12)
The section concerning the *Saucāmaṇi* and other rites, and the section concerning the *Cayana* (piling of the altar) for those performing the *Yajña*.
Sūtra: [The rule applies] to the combination, because the connection with the injunction is purposeful. (29)
Bhāṣya: "Having piled the fire-altar, one should sacrifice with the Saucāmaṇī; having performed the Vājapeya, [one should sacrifice] with the Bṛhaspatisava...

In the Mīmāṃsā system, [there is the injunction]: "One should sacrifice with the Soma. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is this a connection between the subsidiary element (aṅga) and its purpose (prayojana), or is it a conjunction for the sake of time (kāla)? It is a connection between the subsidiary element and its purpose.

For the meaning is directly enjoined by the Vedic text (śruti); otherwise, time would have to be indicated by secondary implication (lakṣaṇā). And when there is a choice between a direct statement and an indication, the direct statement prevails, not the indication. Therefore, the Sautrāmaṇī is a subsidiary part of the Aṅgapraṅga, and the Bṛhaspatisava is a subsidiary part of the Vājapeya.
Sūtra: If it is argued that "time" [is meant] when there is a mention of time. (Grantha) 30.

Bhāṣya: If you view it thus—that there is a relationship between the subsidiary act and its purpose—then why does this not become an injunction of time? For the word "having piled" (*citvā*) is indeed of the nature of an injunction of time [indicating that the action occurs] once the piling (*cayana*) has been completed.
Sūtra: It cannot be so, because there is no inherence with the purpose. (Grantha-nirṇaya 31)

Bhāṣya: This is not so. Because of "non-inherence" (*asamavāya*), there would be no connection between the word and its purpose—that is, the relationship between the word and its meaning—and consequently, there would be no inherence of the *Sautrāmaṇī* with the *Vājapeya*, nor of the *Bṛhaspatisava* with the *Vājapeya*. Furthermore, the context (*prakaraṇa*) would be set aside, as the property of a subordinate part (*aṅgadharma*) is being applied [to the principal].
The sacrifice is understood [as the object], and within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Vājapeya, the Vājapeya itself is understood;

otherwise, in the context of those two, the ritual detail (*dharma*) of something else—the time—would be understood. Therefore, there is a connection between the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and its purpose (*prayojana*). (4.3.13)
The section concerning the subsidiary status of the Vaiśvadeva and other rites to the Full Moon sacrifice and others.
Sūtra: If it is argued that it is for the sake of both [the sacrificer and the deity], (Pūrvapakṣa).

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the scripture states: "Having completed the Paurṇamāsī, one subsequently offers the Vaiśvadeva. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the Vaiśvadeva an auxiliary to both sacrifices, and its connection with the Paurṇamāsī is merely for the sake of time; or is it a relationship between an auxiliary and its primary purpose?
What is established? If this is so, then the Vaiśvadeva serves both purposes. Why? Because it occurs within the context (prakaraṇa).
Chapter 4, Section 3.
Bhāṣya: Because of the force of the scriptural mention of both, and because of the similarity in form with an injunction regarding time, as indicated by the word "having completed" (saṃsthāpya).
Sūtra: Not so, because of the unity of the word. (Siddhānta) || 33 ||

Commentary: There is a single word—"he performs the subsequent offering" (*anunirvapati*). Within a single sentence, it is not possible to enjoin two relationships: that of the Vaimṛdha with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and its relationship with time. For a single sentence is understood to have a single purpose.
Sūtra: If it is argued that [the rule applies] because of the context (prakaraṇa). (Pūrvapakṣa) 34.
The statement made [by the opponent], "Because of the context," must be refuted.
Sūtra: Not so, because of the connection with origination. (Conclusion)

Bhāṣya: This is not so; this very [text] is the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) for the Vaimṛdha sacrifice. It would either form a single syntactical unit with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices due to context (*prakaraṇa*), or it would be directly connected with the Paurṇamāsī.
And in that case, direct connection (*pratyakṣasaṃyoga*) is stronger than context, because of the directness [of the connection].
There is a connection with the full moon day; since it is remote from time, therefore the Vaimṛdha is an auxiliary of the Paurṇamāsī sacrifice. (4.3.14)
The section concerning the timing of the *anuyāja* offerings and others as being subsequent to the *agnimāruta* stotra.
Sūtra: But for one who does not perform [the rite], there would be a lapse of time, because it lacks connection with its purpose.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard: "They proceed with the after-offerings (anuyājas) as a subsidiary (aṅga) to the Āgnimāruta [śastra]," and "Having cast aside the enclosing-sticks (paridhis), he offers the Hāriyojana. Regarding this, there is a doubt:
is a subsidiary being enjoined, or is it time? In the case of the injunction of a subsidiary...

[The opponent argues: "It is direct scriptural statement (*śruti*); [if it were] a prescription of time, there would be figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, it is a prescription of the subsidiary (*aṅga*)—thus [is the prima facie view].
—Page 564— [Mīmāṃsā-Darśana 5.1.10]

We reply: In the statement regarding non-origination, "time" would be the factor; the *agnimāruta* is a subsidiary of the *soma*, and the *anuyāja*s are like those of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*); there is no mutual connection between those two. Likewise, the *paridhi*s are like those of the animal sacrifice, and the *hāriyojana* is a distinct primary [offering]. As for the *anuyāja*s...

The Āgnimāruta [offering] has been reached, but the immediate sequence between those two has not been reached; that is what is being prescribed. Likewise, this applies to the Hāriyojana [offering] and the throwing of the enclosing sticks (paridhi). This being the case, no benefit whatsoever is conferred upon the Hāriyojana by the throwing of the enclosing sticks.
Or [the throwing of the enclosing sticks] is performed with the *hāriyojana* cup. [Objection:

"But surely the throwing of the enclosing sticks is brought to mind because it is an enjoined action. It is replied: No, for the throwing of the enclosing sticks is not to be performed as an enjoined primary act (*bhāvārtha*); rather, this [act of throwing] indeed exists [as a subordinate element].

Is Vaiśvānara permanent (*nitya*), or is he occasional (*naimittika*)? What is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Even now, it is indeed "permanent. This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*): "The fault incurred by not wearing [the sacrificial thread] for a year is destroyed by Vaiśvānara"—thus, its connection with the permanent [rites] becomes consistent. For it is said: "These oblations (*havīṃṣi*) are threefold; these worlds are three; [this is] for the attainment of these worlds. There is no commonality between the worlds and the oblations; if, just as the worlds are permanently three, so too these oblations are permanently three, then the praise through the worlds is logically consistent.
Therefore, Vaiśvānara is indeed eternal.
Sūtra: [The result belongs] to each individual [offering], because of the connection with what has arisen. (Siddhānta) || 13 ||

Commentary: When there is an occasion for what has already arisen, namely the ornamenting of the fire-pan (*ukhā*), there is a conjunction with the removal [of defects]; nor does that which has arisen and is conjoined have the purpose of removing a defect.

Therefore, in this case, as with the curd-offering (*dadhi-homa*), there is no contradiction; thus, it is not an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), but rather something contingent upon an occasion (*naimittika*).

As for what was stated—that because of its eternity, the commonality of the worlds with the people is logical, and not otherwise—that we do not accept; for there will be an explanatory passage (arthavāda) based on the similarity between the three worlds and the oblations. (4.4.6)
The section concerning the fact that the distribution [of sacrificial fees] is contingent upon a specific cause.
Sūtra: [The meditation] on the pot is as before, because it is preceded by that. (Pūrvapakṣa) 14.
Bhāṣya: There is the fire-altar, as it is said, "He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar.
And that—Page 577—Chapter 4, Section 4.
It is heard [in the scripture]: "The year indeed drives him away from his foundation, he who, having piled the fire-altar, does not establish himself. (Bhāṣya 522)
"Thus he stands; he piles five layers of earth"—so it is said.

In this regard, there is a doubt: is this very same permanent fire (*nitya agni*) that is here described as having six layers (*ṣaṭcitika*), or is it a different, occasional fire (*naimittika*) consisting of a single layer (*ekacitika*)? Which [is it]?
Is it attained?— In that very same permanent [altar], this sixth layer is prescribed,

because it is employed specifically for the permanent [altar]; even one who is not otherwise worthy of being established becomes fit to be established by means of this sixth layer— this is the praise of the layering.

For what purpose is it described in this way? Because of the hearing of the word "sixth" (ṣaṣṭhī)—for the sixth is indeed a ordinal number—and the word "sixth" would not be consistent if applied to a single layer of consciousness.
Therefore, the fire-altar consists of six layers; it is eternal.
Sūtra: [The number of oblations] is equal to that [of the Sāmidhenīs], because of the equality of their number. (Yukti 1)
Bhāṣya: There is a "prasaṅkhyāna" (enumerative correspondence) similar to that previously mentioned.
How so? "This earth indeed is the first layer; the plants are the filling soil (purīṣa);
the intermediate space indeed is the second layer; the birds are the filling soil; yonder sky indeed..."

"The third layer is the stars, and the loose soil is the constellations; the atmosphere is indeed the fourth layer, and the quarters are the loose soil; the sacrificer is indeed the fifth layer, and his offspring are the loose soil;
the year is indeed the sixth layer, and the seasons are the loose soil"—thus it is said regarding those that are equal.
And there is a sequence of equal status, as in: "The gods were [born] from the Gandharvas;
from them the Asuras, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas were born"—and by this genitive case, the sequence of these layers (citīs) is likewise treated as equal.
Therefore, it must be equal to this; and if, in the very same sacrifice (*kratu*),
a place is established in five ways by various mixed verses in the sixth explanation of the *lāṅgala* in the *bhūyaprada*, this is the *cit* altar— so says Mādhava.

In the Mīmāṃsā system, these [fires] are those very ones; they are identical to them, and therefore equal to them. For this reason as well, that same eternal fire consists of six layers (ṣaṭcitika). Thus it is concluded.
Sūtra: And because of the appropriateness of the explanatory passage (arthavāda). (Yukti 2) Bhāṣya: There are explanatory passages such as: "There are six layers (citayaḥ), six fillings (purīṣas);
these amount to twelve; twelve months are a year; [it is] the year itself..."

Regarding the statement, "He stands firm"—this does not apply consistently to the fire consisting of a single layer (*ekacitika*). Therefore, the fire must indeed always consist of six layers (*ṣaṭcitika*).
Sūtra: Because there is a single consciousness, [the objection] is raised on account of a specific cause.
17 || (Siddhānta) ||

The Bhāṣya says: “Or rather, there should be a single layer” (this is the occasional [naimittika] rule). Why? Because it is enjoined in the sacrifice by way of a contingency (nimitta), namely, non-establishment; this layer is declared for one who does not establish himself—it is occasional, not obligatory (nitya).
It ought to be so.
Moreover, that [act] is enjoined in relation to the sacrifice (*yāga*), not in relation to the present state; therefore, it cannot exist [simultaneously] with the present. [Objection:
But surely, by the word “having piled” (*citvā*), the reference is to the piling (*cayana*), not to the sacrifice. It is replied:
This is not [to be understood] with reference to the word-meaning as "having piled," but rather with reference to the sentence-meaning:

"having piled the fire-altar"— that is, having accomplished the purpose of piling the fire-altar— and since the purpose of piling the fire-altar is accomplished in the sacrifice, it cannot be otherwise.

And the word "sixth" [is used] because five prior layers have been mentioned; it is perceived only in relation to them. Therefore, it is said that [this occurs] when the sacrifice has been indicated. Consequently, by virtue of this statement, the fire-altar consists of a single layer.
Sūtra: On account of contradiction, there is equality of number with those [qualities]. (18)

Bhāṣya: "And because of the appropriateness of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). (4.1.7) By means of those [eternal verses], there will be the excellence of the two layers having the same preceding [verses]; thus the explanatory passage is made appropriate: "There are five preceding layers; by those layers he does not find firm footing; for this purpose, the sixth [layer]..."
"—let them stand. And even though they are accompanied by the *pūriṣa*, they will constitute twelve in total;
this is because of the "contradiction" between one [set] of six and the number twelve. Even for things that are not equal, a sequential order occurs as if they were equal.
As it is said: "The gods, humans, and ancestors were elsewhere"—(Śrauta Sūtra 4.1.7).
The section concerning the status of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña as an auxiliary part of the [Full-Moon] sacrifice.
Sūtra: The Pitṛyajña, because it has its own specific time, should not be a subordinate part [of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice]. (Conclusion) || 16 ||

Bhāṣya: In the ritual of the new moon (āmāvāsya), there is the Pitṛyajña, according to the text: "On the afternoon of the new moon, they perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the Piṇḍapitṛyajña an auxiliary part (aṅga) of the new moon ritual, or is it not an auxiliary?
Thus [it is asked]: what is the conclusion? It is an auxiliary (*aṅga*), because it is in proximity to that which possesses a fruit and because there is a statement regarding its ransom-price.
[The opponent] says: "But surely, that which lacks a fruit becomes an auxiliary when in proximity to that which possesses a fruit; and this [rite] possesses a fruit."

"By this [injunction], there is also [attainment of] heaven"—thus it is said. It is replied: "True; because of its syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with the new-moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*), heaven cannot be postulated. He says: "Because it expresses time, syntactic unity with the ritual action is not possible. It is replied:

Even by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), syntactical unity with the action is possible; heaven is to be inferred, not indicated, nor is it directly stated (śruti). And thus they declare: "When he performs [the rite] for the ancestors on the preceding day, having thereby redeemed this sacrifice from the ancestors, the sacrificer extends it toward the gods."
—Thus it is heard that [the Pitṛyajña] is to be redeemed at the new moon; therefore, it is a subsidiary part of that [sacrifice].
This being the position reached, we reply: "The Pitṛyajña, because it has its own specific time, should not be a subsidiary."

The Piṇḍapitṛyajña is not an integral part [of the Darśapūrṇamāsa]. Why? Because "it has its own time"—that is, it is connected with a time denoted by its own word, not with a time indicated by the ritual act—as in the case of: "Having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa, one should sacrifice with Soma."

For example, as in the statement: "Thereafter, he performs the Saumya [offering] during the Upasad"—here, this primary term refers only to time and not to the ritual action; regarding the action, it is a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), and direct denotation (śruti) is more powerful than figurative indication. And as for what was said—that there is syntactic unity with the action through figurative indication—[that is refuted].

"It will be so"—but that is not the case. Why? Because figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is appropriate in a restatement (anuvāda), but not in an injunction (vidhi), and this is indeed an injunction; therefore, there is no connection with the New Moon ritual. Thus, at one time, there are two rituals which are independent of each other.
Sūtra: And because the consequence applies equally. (Yukti 1)

The Bhāṣya states: "It is mentioned as being equal to other principal [rites] in the context of the *prasaṅga*: 'There are indeed four great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*s)—the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *jyotiṣṭoma*, and the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*.
Thus, it is mentioned as being on the same footing as the *mahāyajña*s; what is the greatness known from this?"
Could it be that [the fruit] exists from another source? Therefore, it is not a constituent part.
Sūtra: And because it is seen even when [the primary] is prohibited. (Yukti 2)

Furthermore, it is not an auxiliary factor, because when the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*) is prohibited, it indicates the performance of the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*: "One who has rivals should sacrifice only at the full moon, not at the new moon;
having struck down his rival, he should sacrifice with the new moon [sacrifice], and indeed by the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* alone... [the new moon sacrifice is thus indicated].

"By staying overnight, he pleases [the ancestors]"—thus, it shows the Piṇḍapitṛyajña even when the new moon day (Amāvāsyā) has not occurred; this is appropriate only if it is not an auxiliary part [of the Darśa sacrifice]. Therefore, for this reason also, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña is not an auxiliary.

What is the purpose of this reflection? If the installation (*ādhāna*) takes place on the full moon day, then it is not performed on the immediately following new moon day, as in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*);
rather, it must be performed according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). This is another purpose: [regarding] the *kuṇḍa*...
In the *Pāyīnayana*, one performs the *Agnihotra* for a month, [and] for a month with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
— Page 581 — Chapter 4, Section 4.
Bhāṣya: "One should sacrifice"—according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the Piṇḍapitṛyajña should be performed [in that manner];
according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it should not be performed [in that manner]. This is also stated in the Śoka.
They cite: "If the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) occurs on the full moon day, it will be performed after the new moon;
if the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña) is not a constituent part [of that rite], it shall not be performed at that very time."
Thus [ends the section]. (4.4.30)
The section concerning the girdle as a subsidiary element of the sacrificial post.
Sūtra: The rope should be a subordinate part of the animal, because it is prescribed upon the arrival of that [animal]. (Pūrvapakṣa)

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard in the scripture: "Having taken the Āśvina cup and having encircled the sacrificial post with the rope, he dedicates the Savanīya animal to Agni. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is the rope an accessory (aṅga) of the animal, or is it an accessory of the sacrificial post? What [is the conclusion]?

Is it obtained?—“As part of the animal sacrifice. Why? “Because it is prescribed upon its arrival”; for it is prescribed upon the arrival of the animal, as the connection of this [rite] with the animal is heard in the originative injunction:
“Having performed the encircling, one renders service to the animal, and not otherwise. Thus says the Śruti.
[If it were so], there would be an indication (lakṣaṇā) regarding the expression of time— that is, the time would be indicated by means of the wrapping around.
Sūtra: Or rather, it is an auxiliary part of the sacrificial post, because of its being a consecration of that. (Conclusion 23)

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the embellishment of the sacrificial post (yūpa) is indeed directly perceived; for the rope (raśanā) produces firmness in the post, both by its very presence and to whatever extent it extends, and the post has a need for such firmness. Therefore, the rope should belong to the post itself for the sake of its firmness.

Furthermore, the second case-ending occurs only when that [the rope] is the primary element, whereas the third case-ending is used for the rope, and the third case-ending signifies its subordinate status; therefore, it is an accessory (aṅga) of the sacrificial post (yūpa). As for what was stated—that "because it is prescribed upon the arrival of that"—that must be refuted. It is said in reply: the prescription upon the arrival of that...

The sentence and the second case-ending are *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) and direct perception [respectively]; thus, the sentence would have to be sublated.
As for the claim that it is *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication), even indirect indication is indeed logical when a direct statement is impossible.
Sūtra: And the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is for that purpose [of praising], as it possesses meaning. (Yukti 24)
And thus, the meaning of the mantra and the arthavāda will become purposeful: "The youth, well-clothed and girt, has arrived;
he becomes even more excellent as he is born; the wise poets, seeking the gods with their minds, lead him up. Therefore, it is an accessory of the sacrificial post (yūpa).
"Rope"—thus [it is said].
What is the purpose of this deliberation? Here it is heard in scripture: "In a single enclosure, eleven animals are to be tied up. A rope must be provided for each animal, if the former [view] holds.
The prima facie view (*pakṣa*); however, in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), there must indeed be two ropes. They also cite a verse:

"The rope is a limb of the animal; if one were to bind many animals with a single [rope], a separate rope should be used for each animal; if they were in a single enclosure (*yūpa*), there would be a state of having two ropes."
Thus [ends the section] (Jaimini Sūtra 4.4.6).
The section concerning the status of the donkey as a subsidiary part of the animal sacrifice.
Sūtra: And the *svaru* [is part of the sacrificial post] because it is a single portion. (Pūrvapakṣa)

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma which is a subsidiary part of the Soma ritual, as stated: "The initiated one who sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. In that context, it is heard: "He anoints the animal with the *svaru* and the axe. Regarding this, there is a doubt.

"—Is the *svaru* an accessory (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), or is it an accessory of the animal (*paśu*)? What is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? We say: it is an accessory of the sacrificial post. Why? Because of its being a part;
for it is heard in scripture that the *svaru* is a part of the sacrificial post, in the statement: 'He makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post'. (The *svaru*-making ritual)
The meaning is that one should make the sacrificial post (yūpa); thus it becomes a sacrificial post, just as in the case of the *pālāśa* [wood].
Sūtra 526: And the ransom is like its subsidiary part.
(Yukti) --- Page 583 --- Chapter 4, Section 4. 526. Sūtra:
And the ransom is like its subsidiary part. (Yukti)

The statement regarding the ransom-price (*niṣkraya*) shows that the *svaru* is an auxiliary of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), just like the *prastara*. It says: "In former times, O Aśvins, the seers who brought forward the sacrificial post used to praise it after breaking it off, thinking, 'This act is indeed for the sake of the excellence of the sacrifice. They did not see a ransom-price for the *prastara*, [but they saw] the *svaru* of the sacrificial post for the sake of its excellence. From this hearing of the ransom-price, its status as an auxiliary is understood. Therefore, it is an auxiliary of the sacrificial post.
Sūtra: Or rather, it is a subsidiary part of the animal, because it is a purposeful ritual act. (Conclusion) || 29 ||

The Bhāṣya states: "Or rather, it is a subsidiary part of the animal (paśvaṅga). For its purpose is the anointing by means of the *svaru*; thus it is heard in scripture: "He anoints the animal with the *svaru*. That anointing brings about the production of the hair on the animal's back. If this *svaru* is for that purpose, then [its utility] is visible (*dṛṣṭa*).
As for the purpose: if it is for the sake of the sacrificial post, then an invisible (adṛṣṭa) purpose must be inferred from that; therefore, it is an auxiliary to the animal sacrifice.
Sūtra: Through devotion, there may be the statement regarding the price of redemption. (Ābhāsara-Nirṇaya)

By what kind of figurative interpretation (*bhakti*)? He says this: "When the *svaru* is cut off after the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) has already been cut off at the top, by that [act] the sacrificial post itself is as if being cut off; thus, this becomes like a ransom.
It is praise by means of this figurative interpretation.

What is the purpose [of this discussion]? When eleven animals are bound for a single broth (yūṣa), then, according to the prima facie view, the anointing (samañjana) belongs to only one animal; according to the final conclusion (siddhānta), it belongs to all of them. And there is a verse:—

If it is argued that the *svaru* is an accessory (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), then there would be an anointing of only one [post]; but when there are many [posts] for a single sacrificial post, there must be an anointing of all of them. (4.4.29) *Note: The term *samañjana* refers to the ritual act of smearing or anointing.*
"But in the case of all [the others], it is the opposite," is the reading in the Kāśmīra Śrīpura manuscript.

the section concerning the subsidiary status of the Vyāghāra and other rites.
Sūtra: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there are three recitations for the principal offerings, because they are distinguished by others.

The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are established [in the tradition].
